## Upgrade suggestions

### File-exclusion-ban follow-ups (2026-08-29)

- **[measured] The narrowing decides hole-vs-skip on the literal LOOKING like a path, and one live hole does not** — `lint-guard-partial-root.test.ts` writes `!== "check-problem-phrasing-imports"` over a walk of guard IDs. It is an exclusion from a walk, it is spelled at the point of use, and `FILE_LITERAL` cannot see it because a guard id has no slash and no extension. Every walk in this tree that yields something other than a path is outside the rule by construction, and there is no measurement of how many such walks there are.
- **[measured] `!new Set(["a"]).has(x)` is the fourth spelling and nothing bans it** — 23 suites write `!something.has(`, and all 36 occurrences are over a NAMED set, so the inline form is live nowhere today. That is the same "zero offenders" the `!["a"].includes` ban started from the day before it found one, and this spelling is the shortest of the four to reach for.
- **[measured] Three suites now hand-write the same two-assert honesty block** — `analytics-pii`, `check-error` and `guard-scan-dirs` each got "the skipped file is in the walk AND still offends" today, in the same order, in nearly the same words. `assertExemptionsHonest` is that block, and none of them can call it: it takes a LIST and refuses an empty one, and a single-entry hole is a string. The helper's shape assumes the hole is plural.
- **[measured] The `useNativeDriver: true` sweep now matches nothing at all in the walk** — stripping comments removed its one match, which was the exemption's whole subject. It is a sweep asserting an absence over a tree where the shape is extinct, and the only thing proving the reader still works is a separate case naming three adopting files by hand. The `MediaTypeOptions` sweep next to it is in the same position and has no control at all.
- **[inferred] `inline-exclusion.test.ts` walks all 479 suites four times now** — two sweeps and two premise cases, each with its own regex, in one process where `suiteCode` at least caches the reads. The three-suites-three-walks observation filed yesterday is now three suites and six walks, and the premise halves are the copies with the least reason to be separate: both ask "does the tree still write the spelling this rule reads".

### Named-hole follow-ups (2026-08-28 — two closed 2026-08-29)

- **[measured] The ban reads `!["a"].includes(x)` and not the three other spellings of the same decision** — `.filter((x) => x !== "a")`, an early `if (x === "a") continue;`, and a `new Set([...]).has()` all exclude with a literal and none of them match. The metabase hole happened to be written in the one form now banned; the next one has three ways out, and the rule's name promises more than it delivers.
- **[inferred] Naming a hole is checked and nothing checks that the NAME is read** — a suite can lift its literal into `const SKIPPED = [...]` one line above the filter and satisfy this sweep completely. The sharing check shipped today reaches only holes passed as `exempt:` to a sweep call; a hand-rolled filter's named list is still nobody's business.
- **[measured] The premise floor is 15 over 24 membership checks, and `web-security-headers` writes 20 of them** — one suite is five-sixths of the control. If it moves to a helper or a table the floor turns red with nothing wrong, which is a floor measuring one file's style rather than a spelling's currency.
- **[inferred] The suite exempts itself and its own honesty case is the only thing policing that** — the same shape as `offence-sweep.test.ts`, one level smaller, and both are files whose fixture is the thing they ban. It works because the negative control must contain an example; it would stop working the day the control moves to a helper, and nothing would say so.
- **[measured] Three suites now walk all 479 suite files with a regex apiece, in three processes** — this one, the sweep-adoption cases, and the console ban. Each re-reads and re-strips the tree; `suiteCode` caches within a process and nothing carries across. It is seconds, not minutes, and it is the first time the same walk exists three times for three unrelated rules.

### Inline-hole follow-ups (2026-08-28 — one closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `NOT_EVENTS` is an empty list with two assertions about it, and both are vacuous today** — the honesty loop runs zero times and the exclusion in the main loop never fires. It is scaffolding for the next entry rather than a check of anything, which is the honest reading and also means nothing would notice if the honesty loop itself were deleted.
- **[inferred] The audit is now two greps — const names, and inline `.filter`/`.includes` — and neither would see a hole written as an early `continue`** — `if (name === "x") continue;` inside the loop is the same exclusion with no list at all, and it is the shape the metabase one would have taken had it been written one line differently.
- **[measured] Three scans now carry a hand-written "the walk found something" refusal** — gradients, metabase, and the sweeps' own premise. `assertNoOffenders` gives it to twelve callers by construction; these three cannot adopt it (per-element, per-token, per-suite units) and each states it in its own words. A `refuseEmptyScan(count, subject)` would say it once, at the cost of a fourth import in files whose scan is four lines long.
- **[inferred] The taxonomy check tests membership with `taxonomy.includes(`${name}:`)`** — a substring search over the source of `lib/analytics-events.ts`, so a name appearing in a comment, or as a prefix of a longer key followed by a colon, reads as declared. It is the check the suite has always made and the hole-hunting above did not touch it.
- **[measured] Two live stale holes were found today and both had been left by a set that shrank** — the hex-width exemption over a module that stopped spelling the width, and a one-entry exclusion list under a plural comment. Neither was noticed by the suites that own them; both were found by asking a question no case asks. Nothing in the tree runs that question on a schedule.

### Allow-list-audit follow-ups (2026-08-28 — one closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] The audit that found `ALLOWED_LOCAL` was a grep over const NAMES, and a hole named anything else is invisible to it** — sixteen files matched `EXEMPT|ALLOWED|SANCTIONED`; a list called `SKIP`, `KNOWN`, `LEGACY` or spelled inline in a `.filter` was never looked at. The audit is a one-off reading of a naming convention, and nothing in the tree makes the next hole carry one of those three words.
- **[inferred] `coloured` is built for two assertions and is a per-MATCH list with repeats** — a file rendering two gradients appears twice, so it is a count of elements wearing a list of file names. Both readers only ask "is this file in it" and "is it non-empty", which is true of the shape by accident rather than by design.
- **[measured] The gradient scan now states both refusals by hand, which is the third copy of that paragraph in this tree** — `assertNoOffenders` gives them by construction to twelve callers; this walk cannot adopt it because its unit is the element. The doc block records that shape as needing a different walk, and this is now the second scan that wrote the refusals out instead.
- **[inferred] The floor on the scan is "more than zero", where the sweeps' equivalent is "the walk found files"** — a repo whose only remaining coloured gradient is the allow-listed one passes both new assertions while the rule has stopped being about anything. The honest floor is two (one allowed, one shared recipe), and it is not obvious that number stays true.
- **[measured] `assertExemptionsHonest` is called 14 times across 9 suites and 5 more holes are policed by a hand-written `assert.match` loop** — the helper exists to be the one place the "is this still needed" question is asked, and a third of the tree's holes ask it themselves, mostly because their `stillNeeded` is a regex over a file the helper's walk does not carry.

### Per-hole-reader follow-ups (2026-08-28 — one closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] A rule with two holes and one reader is reported TWICE, once per call, and the two entries are identical** — `privacy-translated-section.test.ts: WHOLE_STRING_HEX_RUN` appeared twice in the mutation run, because neither call can be named as the policed one. That is honest and it is also a diff that says one thing in two lines; an entry that carried the exempt list, or the call's index, would tell the reader which sweep to go and look at.
- **[inferred] `readers >= holes` counts readers that may all belong to one hole** — three reads of a rule and three exempt-carrying calls satisfies it even when every read is inside the same case. The arithmetic went from "a name with one reader" to "a name with enough readers" and the property wanted is still per-call, which nothing short of block structure can see.
- **[measured] The stale exemption survived because a hole with no honesty case is invisible to every check in this tree** — `assertExemptionsHonest` polices lists that ASK it to; a bare `exempt:` on a sweep call answers to nothing. The new arithmetic catches it only when the rule is shared elsewhere; a single-call sweep with a bare `exempt` and one reader still passes with a hole nobody asks about.
- **[inferred] Removing the exemption widened the sweep to a module it had never walked** — it passes today, and the reasoning that put it there ("the declaring module may spell the width") becomes true again the moment somebody inlines the pattern for readability. The case that would catch that is the sweep itself, which is the right answer and means the failure will read as a new offence rather than as a returning exemption.
- **[measured] `sourceCode` strips comments and that is what made the exemption look needed** — the doc comment in the declaring module quotes `/^[0-9a-f]{16}$/` to explain what was retired, so a human reading the file sees the offence and the sweep does not. Every "still needed?" judgement in this tree is made against stripped source while being written by someone reading the raw file.

### Stale-entry follow-ups (2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `unseen` refuses an entry the walk never met and cannot refuse one that is merely WRONG** — `"hero-banner.test.ts: SOLID_HERO"` is checked against the calls found, so a rename is caught; an entry naming a real exempt call whose exemption reasoning has since stopped being true is indistinguishable from a correct one. The only external check on the reasoning is the paragraph above the list, read by a human.
- **[inferred] The export check reads `export function` and the module also exports a TYPE** — `OffenceRule` is deliberately outside the adoption names because a type is not a call, and the regex expresses that by accident rather than by saying so: `export type` simply does not match `export function`. A future `export const` helper (a prebuilt rule, say) is a third shape the check would silently not read.
- **[measured] `sweepingSuites` and `adoptingSuites` differ by exactly one name and their walks are identical otherwise** — two functions, one `suiteFiles().filter`, differing in which regex they build. It is the honest split (the call readers must not walk the wide set) and it is also two names a reader has to hold apart, in a file where "adopter" already meant three different counts this week.
- **[inferred] The premise floor on the export check is 3, which is every export the module has** — a floor with no slack, deliberately, since deleting an export is the thing the check exists to notice; it means removing a genuinely dead export fails here first and reads as a broken regex rather than as an intentional deletion.
- **[measured] The sharing check's `seen` list is built for one consumer and is the only full inventory of exempt-carrying sweep calls in the tree** — four entries today. Nothing else can ask "which sweeps have holes", so the honesty floor and the `unseen` refusal both re-derive it inside the same case rather than either being able to read it from anywhere.

### Call-reader follow-ups (2026-08-28 — two closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `sweepCalls` bounds a call at the first `})` after its opening bracket** — which is exactly right for every call in this tree and wrong for the first one that nests an object in its options (a `read` written as an arrow closing over a map, an `exempt` built inline from an object). The bound cuts such a call in half, the rule falls out of the slice, and the call is reported as unreadable — loud rather than silent, which is the trade this reader was built to make, and still a false failure a caller cannot fix except by reformatting.
- **[inferred] The sharing check counts identifier occurrences over the WHOLE suite, not within the case** — a rule read a second time three hundred lines away, in an unrelated `it`, satisfies it exactly as a read in the exemption assert below the sweep does. The property it can actually see is "this name has more than one reader"; the property it is for is "the case policing the hole asks through the rule", and nothing here can tell those apart without parsing the block structure.
- **[measured] `POLICED_OTHERWISE` is one entry and it is a string pairing two names** — `"hero-banner.test.ts: SOLID_HERO"` is matched by exact equality against a string built the same way, so renaming either half silently empties the exemption and turns the sharing case red with a real-looking failure. Every other exemption list in this tree names a FILE, which the walk itself would refuse if it went missing.
- **[inferred] The readability case now has two derived halves and no floor of its own** — it stands entirely on `adoptingSuites()`, whose floor is asserted in the case above it. That is the right place for the number and it means the two cases fail together when the adopter walk breaks, so the second failure is noise on a red run and the only signal on the day the walk and the reader disagree.
- **[measured] The exempt-carrying floor is 4 with one row of slack, and it counts CALLS while the adopter floor counts SUITES** — two floors, two units, one paragraph apart. `npm run remeasure-floors` knows about neither, which is now the fifth suite-local floor in this tree whose number is the current count minus some slack.

### Named-rule follow-ups (2026-08-28 — two closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] The named-rule case reads the call with a regex over collapsed source, which is the shape it exists to distrust** — it finds `assertNoOffenders({ rule: X, files:` and nothing else, so a call written with `files` before `rule`, or built from a spread options object, is invisible to it. The premise floor of nine is what stands between that and a silent pass, and the floor is the current count with no slack.
- **[inferred] Naming the rule makes sharing POSSIBLE and nothing checks that it happened** — `hero-banner` shares its const between the sweep and the exemption assert because this change did it by hand; a sixth sweep can name its rule and still write the recipe out again in the assert below. The check is one step short of the property it is for.
- **[measured] Four rules were named for a second reader that does not exist yet** — the two gradients sweeps and the `TAG_COLORS` allowlist carry no `exempt` list, so their const has exactly one reader today. The argument is that a rule needing a name is discovered at the moment somebody adds an exemption, which is the worst moment to be re-typing a recipe; the cost is four names that currently read as ceremony.
- **[inferred] `INLINE_HERO_TRIPLET` and `INLINE_PHOTO_SCRIM` are named for what OFFENDS, and `DECLARES_TAG_COLORS` for what is SANCTIONED** — which is right for each shape (one is `assertNoOffenders`, one is `assertOnlyTheseMatch`) and means the two exports' rules are read in opposite polarity under the same parameter name. Nothing says so at the call site.
- **[measured] The eyebrow recipe is a four-line regex matching a formatted style block, and it is the sweep most sensitive to prettier** — `\s*\n\s*` between each property assumes one declaration per line in that order. A reordered style object stops matching and the sweep reports a clean tree; the exemption assert would catch it now, which is a side effect of the sharing rather than a check anybody wrote.

### Conjunct-rule follow-ups (2026-08-28 — two closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `OffenceRule` is a union whose array arm has no way to say OR** — every list is a conjunction, which is what all three blocked sweeps needed and is a choice the type does not state. A rule that wants "reads the source AND (counts six OR counts seven)" writes the disjunction back into one pattern with an alternation, which is where these rules came from.
- **[inferred] `matchesRule` is exported so an exemption can ask the sweep's question, and nothing makes an exemption use it** — measured 2026-08-28: of the four sweeps carrying an `exempt` list, `dashboard-banner` and `privacy-translated-section` already shared a const, `i18n-locales-helper` now goes through `matchesRule`, and `hero-banner` was the one writing its recipe out twice (closed the same day). What remains is that nothing enforces the sharing: naming the rule is checked, using the name in the exemption assert is not.
- **[measured] The empty-conjunct refusal is the third hazard and the only one no caller has ever hit** — the two original refusals were each written against a real near-miss in this tree; this one is reasoned from `every([])`. It costs three lines and a case, and it is the first refusal here that is speculative rather than measured.
- **[inferred] The g/y refusal now names `pattern.source`, which is untruncated** — a compound rule with a long conjunct prints the whole thing into the failure. The two shipped compound conjuncts are 14 and 22 characters; nothing caps it, and the same message is the one a reader meets when their sweep is already broken.
- **[measured] The adopter floor is 9 and counts suites naming either export; `matchesRule` is a third name it does not count** — a suite that imports only `matchesRule` (an exemption case reusing a sweep's rule) reads as a non-adopter, which is right today and would be wrong the moment a rule is shared between a sweep in one file and an exemption in another.

### Access-builder follow-ups (2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `consoleSwapFixture` now takes a union whose two arms are told apart by `typeof`** — a bare string is the dotted form and an object is the bracket form, which reads fine in the four call shapes the table uses and has no room for a fifth. A `console?.warn = x` or a private-field spelling arrives as neither arm, and the honest options are a third arm (a union that grows with the grammar) or a raw access string (which puts the leading `.` back in the caller's hands, where forgetting it silently produces `consolewarn` — a must-match row that stops matching).
- **[inferred] The builder's four spellings are pinned by a case that writes them out through `CONSOLE_IDENTIFIER`** — so the assertion and the implementation say the same thing in the same two pieces, and a reader cannot tell which one is the specification. It catches the mutation it was written for (every bracket row collapsing to the dotted form) and it would not catch the two of them drifting together, which is the shape a shared constant always has.
- **[measured] `CONSOLE_IDENTIFIER` is exported from `lib/` and read by six fixture rows and two suites, none of which ship** — the same trade the table itself has, one level smaller: it must live here because `CONSOLE_SWAP_PROBE` is built from it and the probe DOES ship, so the choice is a shipped constant with two shipped readers and eight test-only ones, or a second join in `__tests__/helpers/`. Worth writing down that the table's location argument is now load-bearing for a second export.
- **[inferred] The whole-file case derives its expectation from the same `offends` field the row-by-row walk asserts** — which is what keeps it from drifting and also means a row whose `offends` is simply WRONG passes both walks and the new one identically. Nothing in this tree checks a fixture's verdict against anything but the rule the fixture exists to describe; the only external check is a human reading `why`.
- **[measured] The premise case now has three floors and one equality, and only the two counts have their slack written down** — the duplicate-line equality is exact, the five-a-side floors say "two rows of slack each way", and the reason the floors are floors (a row deleted is an ordinary edit) is stated once for both. A fourth suite-local floor would restate the same paragraph; `npm run remeasure-floors` still cannot see any of them.

### Shared-refusal follow-ups (2026-08-28 — one closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `refuseUnsweepableInput` takes five parameters to check two things, and two of them exist only to keep a noun** — `skipped` and `vacuously` are per-shape strings threaded through a shared function so that the shared function can say something unshared. It is the honest version of the trade and it is also the shape that argues for having left the two `assert.ok`s where they were: the check is four lines and the plumbing to share it is five parameters and a doc block.
- **[inferred] A third sweep shape would have to invent its own two nouns before it could use the refusal** — the helper now assumes every shape can phrase "what a stateful rule skips" and "what an empty walk proves". A predicate-rule shape (the one three sweeps still cannot adopt) skips *files*, not offenders or matches, and its empty walk proves something the current `vacuously` wording has no slot for.
- **[measured] The labelled-problem strings interpolate `what` into the entry AND into the message** — so a caller's phrase appears once per unsanctioned file plus once in the sentence, and a long `what` makes the diff wider than the paths it is labelling. The two shipped callers pass four and five words; nothing caps it.
- **[inferred] `assertNoOffenders` reports its offenders as a bare path list and the other shape now labels its entries** — one of the two shapes has a self-describing diff and one does not. The offender shape has only one kind of problem so a label would be noise, which is right and also means the two failures no longer look like they came from the same module.
- **[measured] The rename left `instead:` in four unrelated places that read as the same idea** — `dead-i18n-keys.test.ts` carries a `readonly instead: string` field documented as "what a contributor who trips this should do instead", and two other suites build failure messages ending "use X instead:". The parameter this change unified is now spelled `what` and the neighbouring concept is still `instead`, which is the same collision one level out.

### Fixture-table follow-ups (2026-08-28 — three closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `CONSOLE_SWAP_FIXTURES` lives in `lib/` and is read by nothing that ships** — the module is the app's own source tree, and the table exists entirely for two suites. It is there because the guard sweeps `lib/` and the fixtures must be built without the banned literal, which is a property of THIS module rather than of the fixtures; `__tests__/helpers/` is where every other shared fixture in this tree lives and would need the joined-literal trick restated once. The trade is a shipped constant with no shipped reader versus a fourth copy of the one thing this change removed.
- **[inferred] The two walks assert the same table with different operators and neither says the other exists** — the guard's suite calls `findConsoleSwaps(...).length`, the ban's calls `assert.match`/`doesNotMatch`, and a reader who fixes one failure has no reason to expect the second. They fail together on every mutation tried, so the second failure is noise on a red run and the only signal on the day the scanner and the pattern disagree — which is the case worth having and the one nothing states.
- **[measured] The premise case pins "at least five a side" over a table of 7 and 7** — a floor with two rows of slack on each half, chosen so an ordinary row deletion does not turn a case about vacuity. It is also the third floor in this tree whose number is "the current count minus some slack" with the slack unstated; `npm run remeasure-floors` exists for exactly that arithmetic and does not know about test-local floors.
- **[inferred] `why` is prose in a data table and is read only by failure messages** — so a row whose `why` no longer describes its `line` is invisible until something fails, and at that point the message is the thing being trusted. Every other rendering table in this tree (`IRREGULAR_KINDS`, `LINT_GUARDS`) has the same shape and the same exposure; what is different here is that these strings are the only statement of WHY each row's verdict is the right one.
- **[measured] `consoleSwapFixture` takes a property name and always emits `= () => {};`** — the arrow is the seam-shaped right-hand side, which is what a real swap looks like, and it means the four bracket-form rows cannot use the helper and are written out. Half the table goes through the shared builder and half repeats the `${CONSOLE}` interpolation, which is the shape "one trick, stated once" was meant to end.

### Boundary follow-ups (2026-08-27 — three closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] The console rule's negative side is now asserted in two suites and they do not agree on what it covers** — the guard's suite pins the read form, the comparison form and (new) the wrapper form; the ban's suite pins three lines chosen to be the ones a widening would break. Neither is derived from the other and both will drift, which is the same two-copies problem the shared pattern just solved one level up. The honest fix is one exported fixture table of must-match/must-not-match lines that both suites walk.
- **[inferred] `\bconsole` still matches `window.console.log = x` and `globalThis.console.warn = x`** — correct, since both ARE the global, and it is now the only spelling of the subject the pattern accepts loosely. Worth a case saying so, because the boundary case reads as "the identifier must be exactly console" and the truth is "the identifier must END at console".
- **[measured] Four strings say what the rule is and they are written in four files** — the scanner's heading, the wrapper's clean-tree line, the probe refusal and the `LINT_GUARDS` blurb. This change edited all four by hand to keep one sentence true; a fifth reader would make it five. The check name is already shared, and the noun phrase ("a property of the global console") could be too.
- **[inferred] The 62-key four-locale translation backlog is closed and the suggestion that named it is still open** — the measurement today is 4 keys reading as English in all four locales, and all four are legitimately identical (`profileIdPlaceholder`, `templateHotWheelsName`, and two pure formatters). The per-locale endgame the 2026-08-22 entry predicted happened; what is left is deciding whether a "same as English" report should exist at all, since its honest answer will now always be a handful of proper nouns.
- **[measured] `npm test` is 6744 cases and the four-leg `verify` takes minutes on a cold `node_modules`** — the suites are process-per-file and the sweeps re-walk the tree in each, which the shared caches make cheap WITHIN a process and not across them. Nothing here is slow enough to fix today; it is the first run where the count crossed a number worth writing down.

### Allowlist-sweep follow-ups (2026-08-27 — four closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] `assertOnlyTheseMatch` and `assertNoOffenders` share two refusals written twice, word for word apart from one noun** — the g/y check and the empty-walk check are copy-pasted between the two exports, differing only in "skips offenders" versus "skips matches". A private `refuseUnsweepableInput(rule, files, subject)` would say each once; what argues against is that the two messages are the only place each shape's failure is phrased in its own terms.
- **[inferred] The new helper reports both directions in ONE `deepEqual` over a `{unexpected, missing}` object** — so a failure prints an object diff and then the sentence, and the reader meets the structure before the explanation. Two asserts would each fail with their own message and stop at the first, which loses the second half of the answer on a run where both are wrong.
- **[measured] Three of the four sweeps that could still adopt cannot, for three different reasons** — `i18n-locales-helper`'s offence is a compound predicate (an `includes` and a regex), the LinearGradient scan is per-MATCH rather than per-file, and `dead-i18n-keys`/`link-aschild-style-flatten` push offenders from a line loop. A `rule: RegExp | ((source: string) => boolean)` would take the first, at the cost of the g/y refusal being meaningless for half the callers.
- **[inferred] `what` and `instead` are the same parameter under two names** — both finish "these {subject} …", and the two helpers disagree about what to call it. A caller writing their second sweep this week gets it wrong once. The names were chosen to read correctly in each message ("these modules statically import…" versus "these files re-declare…"), which is a real difference and a thin one.
- **[measured] The adopter floor is now 8 and the helper module is imported by nine files** — the floor counts suites whose CODE names either export, so the two declaring files are excluded by name rather than derived. A third declaring file (a second helper built on this one) joins the adopter count without adopting anything.

### Adopted-sweep follow-ups (2026-08-27 — three closed 2026-08-28)

- **[measured] Three of the five adopters pass an `exempt` list and none of them is policed by `assertExemptionsHonest`** — each got a hand-written case instead, and the three cases ask three different questions: does the exempt file still match the rule (dashboard, twice), does it still declare the thing the rule protects (hero solid), and nothing at all for the eyebrow, whose exemption is proved by a separate case one screen up. The shared helper for exactly this exists and takes a `stillNeeded` predicate; the reason it was not used is that its report is built for a LIST of holes and these are one or two apiece.
- **[inferred] The chevron rule now allows 160 characters between `<Text` and the glyph, and nothing says what that number is for** — it is "an inline style object with a spread and a colour", measured off the two files that have one. A third row with a longer style object reads as clean, which is the same silent-miss the `[^}]*` version had, one size up. A rule matching the glyph inside any styled `<Text>` regardless of distance would need a different anchor rather than a bigger number.
- **[measured] Four of the five adopted sweeps now name their rule in a `const` and one still inlines it** — the two gradients sweeps pass the literal straight to the helper, while the hero and chevron rules were lifted so their honesty case could reuse them. Both readings are fine and the file no longer says which it prefers; the difference is invisible until someone adds the sixth sweep and picks by whichever neighbour they read first.

### One-matcher follow-ups (2026-08-27 — three closed 2026-08-27, one 2026-08-28)

- **[inferred] The word-counting floor would miscount a stream whose name is a substring of an identifier the helper legitimately has** — `\bdebug\b` is safe against `debugging` and not against a local called `debug`, and the five names are five of the most ordinary words a helper could reach for. The floor's message says which spellings it counts, so a false positive reads clearly; it is still a rule that would push back on a variable name for reasons the person naming it did not sign up for.
- **[measured] Four files now build a console fixture through a joined or aliased literal, up from three** — the guard's probe, `check-console-swap.test.ts`'s `C`, `guard-report-paths.test.ts`'s planted offender, and now `default-console-seams.test.ts`'s `CONSOLE`. Each says why it is joined; the fourth is the point at which "everyone works around the exemption-free ban the same way" is worth one exported `consoleSwapFixture(method)` rather than four independent explanations of one trick.

### Mapped-stream follow-ups (2026-08-27 — three closed 2026-08-27)

- **[DONE 2026-08-23, the same split] `lib/privacy-baseline-provenance.ts` now imports `privacy-page` for the language list and `privacy-body-baselines` for the path helper, and the second already imports the first** — so the module reaches the same constant through two paths. Harmless, and it is the shape that makes an import cycle when somebody moves the helper; re-exporting the list from `privacy-body-baselines`, or splitting the list into its own module as the run below suggested, removes the second path.

A shape-half rule ("this table has a key no page is published for") would turn the backstop into a report, and would fire before any drift call rather than only when that key's value happened to move.
- **[DONE 2026-08-23, `as const satisfies`] `PRIVACY_PAGE_LANGUAGES` is now the closed set three modules validate against and it is still a bare `readonly {code: string}[]`** — so the type system knows nothing about it and every check is a runtime `some`. A `PrivacyPageLanguageCode` union derived from the literal would make `privacyPolicySourcePath` refuse `"de-DE"` at compile time in the three call sites that pass a known constant, and leave the throw for the ones that pass a table key.
- **[DONE 2026-08-23, `lib/privacy-languages.ts`] Four of the six privacy modules now import `privacy-page` only for its language list** — `privacy-body-baselines`, `privacy-translated-section`, `privacy-translation-provenance` and `scrub-promise-provenance`. `privacy-page` also carries the HTML renderer, the CSP string and the language picker, so four provenance modules pull a page renderer into their import graph to ask which six codes exist. Splitting the list into its own module is the kind of change that is cheap now and awkward once something bundles one of them.
- **[DONE 2026-08-23, `changedFilesRefusal`] Every provenance evaluator validates its inputs and none validates `changedFiles`** — the list arrives from `git diff --name-only` and is trusted to be repo-relative posix paths. A caller that passed absolute paths, or output from a `git diff` run in a subdirectory, would find nothing in the set and every value would read as unbacked; the guard would report six failures naming files the reader can see in their own diff. One assertion that no entry starts with `/` or `.` would make that a stopped run with a reason.
- **[measured] The refusal message lists the known codes and the six-code list is now spelled in a message, a picker, a floor table and three parity cases** — which is derivation working, since all six read the same constant. Worth knowing that the message's length now grows with the language count: at fifteen locales the refusal is a paragraph, and the useful half is the first sentence.

The property is real and the cover is at the wrong altitude: extracting the "which reports, in what order, to which stream" decision into a pure function over outcomes would let one call assert it, and would leave the scratch repository for the git questions only it can answer.

Deriving the forbidden strings from `PROVENANCE_TABLES` the way the ordering case does would cost four lines and remove the coupling.

The languages are a closed set (`PRIVACY_PAGE_LANGUAGES`); a parameter typed to it, or a throw on an unknown code, turns a silent wrong answer into a stopped run.
- **[measured] Three suites now read `lib/provenance-tables.ts` for different reasons and one of them is a script test** — the registry is imported by the script, by its own suite, and now by the script's suite, which makes it the third-most-imported module in the guard family after two weeks of existence. That is the shape working, and it is worth knowing that a change to `ProvenanceTable` now moves three files rather than one.

### Third-table follow-ups (2026-08-23)

This is the merge the third module deliberately did not do, and it is now a merge of three rather than an invention from two.

- **[DONE 2026-08-23, two cases] The registry's ordering is now load-bearing over three entries and stated only in a comment** — reports print in declaration order and the first `unparseable` stops the run before any report prints, so a mangled baselines module still suppresses two reports that would have been fine. Filed once before this table landed and worth more now: a case asserting reporting order matches declaration order is four lines.

They fail for different reasons and their messages read alike. A cross-reference in both would stop the next reader deleting the smaller one as a duplicate, which is the same note the scrubber suites already needed.

Worth watching: the moment a third question arrives, the file is a suite about `PRIVACY.md` rather than about the scrubber, and the split is cheaper before that than after.

- **[measured] The registry is a list and the script is the only thing that reads it, so the ORDER it declares is load-bearing and stated only in a comment** — reports print in list order, and the first `unparseable` is the one that stops the run before any report is printed. Today that means a mangled baselines module suppresses a translation report that would have been fine. That is the shipped behaviour and it was the shipped behaviour before the refactor, but it is now a property of an array literal rather than of two statements in sequence, which is a much easier thing to reorder by accident. A case asserting the reporting order matches the declaration order would cost four lines.
- **[inferred] `provenanceRegistryRefusal` runs inside `main`, so an empty registry is caught at RUN time and never at build time** — the check is right and it fires late: `lint:all` is where somebody notices, on CI, after a build. The same claim as a module-level assertion (or a case in the suite, which is what actually exists today) catches it in `npm test`, which is where the person who emptied the registry is standing. Worth deciding which of the two is the real guard, since two guards for one claim is how one of them stops being maintained.
- **[DONE 2026-08-23, the classification pinned; the wording rule is not reachable] Every table's `driftSkipped` and `unparseable` sentence is a template literal in the registry, and the two tables' wordings are now three lines apart** — which is what makes them comparable, and it is also how they converge. The existing case requires the skip lines to DIFFER and to name their own module; nothing says the same about the two `unparseable` sentences, because only one table can produce one. The day a second table asks for the three-way classification, the second sentence will be written by copying the first, and the case that would have caught it does not exist yet.
- **[REJECTED 2026-08-23 on inspection: the cheap version the entry proposes already exists. "round-trips each table's own module source back to the table it ships" parses each entry's named module and requires the outcome to be `evaluated`, clean, and `driftSkipped: null` — a path holding no table fails it as `unparseable` for the one entry and as a non-null skip line for the other two. A reference-equality case would add nothing that case does not already catch.] The registry names module paths as strings and the guard hands them to `git cat-file`, so a renamed module is a silent skip until somebody reads the log** — the suite asserts each path exists in THIS checkout, which catches the rename at test time. It does not catch the subtler one: a path that exists but no longer holds the table, which classifies as `unparseable` for one entry and as `absent` — a skip — for the other. Deriving the path from the module's own import rather than restating it would close it, and would need a build step this repo does not have; the honest cheap version is a case asserting each entry's `current` is reference-equal to the export its `module` names.
- **[DONE 2026-08-23, a paragraph on the field] `changedFiles` is now read once and shared by every table, which is right and quietly widens what each table sees** — before, each pass asked for its own diff and could in principle have asked a narrower question. Nothing did, and nothing plans to; the observation is that "which files the diff touched" is now a guard-level fact rather than a table-level one, so a future table wanting a path-filtered view of it has to change the loop rather than its own entry. Worth a sentence in `ProvenanceBaseRevision` saying the list is deliberately unfiltered.

The other direction would pull `lib/i18n-source.ts` and `lib/js-tokens.ts` into the bundle through `app/settings.tsx`, and the only thing recording that is a comment at the import site. `bundle-size` would catch it late, as a number rather than as a name, and the repo already runs `check-analytics-imports` for exactly this shape of rule.

The band case stays green with a locale parked at 90.1% indefinitely, which is a milder version of the exact condition the last fifteen runs spent themselves ending. If the state is a transition, something should say what it is transitioning from and roughly when it started; a date next to the name is the cheapest version.
- **[measured] The two lists carry three rules between them and the app reads one boolean** — `app/settings.tsx` calls `isPartiallyTranslated` and renders a badge; `COMPLETE_LANGUAGES`, `TRANSLATION_FLOORS` and `localeListingState` are all test-side, as is every percentage this programme publishes. That ratio is not a criticism — the machinery is what stopped the drift — but nobody has asked in a while what the READER gets from it. Six locales at 100% is a fact the picker still does not say out loud, and the badge is the only place it could.

### Completeness-rule follow-ups (2026-08-22)

- **[DONE 2026-08-22, `localeListingState`] `COMPLETE_LANGUAGES` and `PARTIALLY_TRANSLATED_LANGUAGES` are two lists over the same six names, and neither knows about the other** — one says "finished, may not slip", the other says "unfinished, badge it", and today they partition the picker exactly. Nothing checks that: a locale in both would be badged as partial while a rule swears it declares everything, and a locale in neither is unprotected AND unqualified, which is the state a seventh language passes through legitimately. One case comparing the two against the measurement would say which of the three states each locale is in and refuse the impossible one.
- **[inferred] The completeness rule makes the map's SIZE the thing under pressure, and nothing measures that** — every new English key now costs six values, so the cheapest way to stay green is to not add keys, which is right up to the point where somebody reuses a near-miss key rather than writing the honest one. `variants`/`variantsLabel` and `searchFilterItems`/`searchResultsItems` are already the tree's evidence that near-misses get created; the new pressure is toward the opposite mistake. A count of base keys over time, published rather than gated, would show which way it is going.
- **[measured] The rule fires on the base map growing, and the base map grew 38 times this week** — 501 keys today against 538 before the dead-key removals, with families added and removed throughout. That is the churn rate the ceiling now sits on top of, and it is the number that decides whether this rule is cheap or a chore. Worth re-reading in a week: if `COMPLETE_LANGUAGES` has not been touched and no PR complained, the trade was right; if a name came off it, the trade was not.
- **[inferred] Six locales at 100% means the app can now claim something in the store listing it could not claim before** — `APPSTORE-SUBMISSION.md` and the localisation metadata are a separate tree from `lib/i18n-context.tsx`, and nothing connects the coverage measurement to what the listing says a language is. The measurement is now a fact worth publishing outside the repository, and the place it would be wrong is the place nobody checks.
- **[DONE 2026-08-22, `PRIVACY_TRANSLATION_SOURCES`] `PRIVACY.md` has six translations as separate files and no coverage rule touches them at all** — `PRIVACY.md.be`, `.de`, `.es`, `.pl`, `.ru` are prose, so the key-counting machinery cannot see them, and a policy change in English would ship five stale translations with nothing red. It is the same defect class the whole i18n programme just closed, one directory over, and the honest unit there is a per-file checksum of the English source recorded next to each translation.

### Sweep-finished follow-ups (2026-08-22)

- **[DONE 2026-08-22, `COMPLETE_LANGUAGES`] Every i18n rule in the tree is now green by arithmetic, and none of them would notice the next English key** — six locales at 100%, so the thirteen family entries, the two floors tables and the coverage report all assert things nothing can currently fail. What the repo has never had is the rule that matters from here: a key added to `en` and not to the other five. `TRANSLATION_FLOORS` argues against it at length (a ceiling on `inherited` goes red on every feature PR, before the translations land) and that argument was written when four locales were 200 keys behind. At zero behind, the cost of the ceiling is one PR's worth of lag rather than a permanent red, and the trade is worth re-opening on its own terms rather than inheriting the old answer.
- **[measured] `de.selectedCount` is the only count-bearing value in the map shaped differently from its five siblings, and the reason is a guard** — `ausgewählt` does not inflect, so `1 ausgewählt` needs an INVARIANT entry in the agreement suite and `Ausgewählt: 5` needs nothing. Both are correct German; the second was chosen partly because it costs no exemption. Worth noticing as a pressure the guard exerts on the copy: a rule that is cheap to satisfy one way will get satisfied that way, and nobody records that the shape was a guard's idea. The comment at the call site is the mitigation, not the fix.
- **[inferred] `PARTIALLY_TRANSLATED_LANGUAGES` is empty and `languagePartial`/`languagePartialHint` are now strings no user can reach** — translated into six locales, rendered by a branch that cannot be true. The orphan guard counts them as read (settings.tsx names them), the dead-key sweep would not flag them, and they are exactly the kind of thing the next dead-key run deletes correctly-looking and wrongly. The structural case added today pins the caller; nothing pins the two KEYS, and a one-line note in `UNTRANSLATABLE_KEYS`-style prose next to them would survive the sweep that the case does not cover.
- **[measured] The whole translation programme is now measurable as one number and nobody is measuring it** — eight prefix families, five screen families, one denominator exemption, one per-locale sweep, across roughly fifteen runs, ending at 498/498 in six languages. The tables that got it there (`FAMILIES`, `TRANSLATION_FLOORS`, the screen list) each carry the reasoning for one step and none of them says what the programme was or that it finished. A short note in `lib/i18n-coverage.ts` — what the units were, in order, and which ran out when — is what stops the next locale being started by re-deriving the same five units.
- **[inferred] A seventh language would arrive at 0% and every one of those tables would have to be edited by hand** — `TRANSLATION_LANGUAGES`, `TRANSLATION_FLOORS` (exhaustive, so it is a compile error, which is right), `PARTIALLY_TRANSLATED_LANGUAGES` (a red parity case, also right), the quotation-mark table, the German-register suite's assumption that exactly one locale is German, and the agreement suite's choice of which plural rule a language needs. Six edits, four of which fail loudly and two of which do not. Worth listing in one place before somebody adds Ukrainian and finds the two quiet ones by shipping.

### Per-locale-sweep follow-ups (2026-08-22)

- **[measured] `pl` was 67 keys behind while `be` was 62, and no report in this repo could name the five** — `addFriend`, `removeFriend`, `follow`, `unfollow`, `saveCollection`: social verbs `be` translated days ago and `pl` never did. Every count published here is per-LOCALE (a percentage that averages five keys away) or per-KEY across all four partials (the "English in all four" filter, which drops a key the moment ONE locale translates it). A key three locales have and the fourth does not falls between both, and it is the shape a per-locale sweep meets last. One report — "keys declared in some locales and not others, by locale" — would name the whole class, and the parser already returns everything it needs.
- **[measured] The verbatim guard's first run is ten exemptions and zero findings, which is what a rule written AFTER the work looks like** — every English-verbatim value in the tree turned out legitimate (a brand, four loanwords, `Premium`, an example handle, two wordless strings). The risk is specific and worth naming now: a guard whose visible content is an exemption list reads as a list of things somebody gave up on, and the next reader deletes it or adds to it. It earns its keep on the NEXT bulk sweep, not this one. Whatever the endgame does with the families table should keep this one.
- **[measured] `de` holds seven of the ten verbatim keys and `ru`/`be` two each, and the number measures LANGUAGE DISTANCE rather than care** — German legitimately keeps `Comics`, `Chat`, `Chats`, `Tags`, `Optional`, `Premium`; Belarusian keeps a brand and a handle. A reader who meets the exemption list sorted by locale would draw exactly the wrong conclusion about which translation was done more carefully. If that list ever gets published as a report, it needs the sentence.
- **[inferred] Three suites now read locale VALUES with three conventions, and `readableText` only unified two** — `i18n-english-verbatim` and `i18n-complete-families` share it via `helpers/i18n-readable-text.ts`; `i18n-quotation-marks` scans `block.body` as raw text and `i18n-agreement` scans `block.values` as raw spans. All three are asking "what does this locale SAY", and two of them would report a mark or a plural inside a comment or an identifier if either ever appeared. Not a defect today; it is the same one-reader argument `helpers/i18n-source-file.ts` already won at the file level, arriving one level down.
- **[inferred] Four of six locales are now complete, so every listed family is all-green by construction for them and the family suite only says anything about `de` and `es`** — thirteen entries, each with a `because` paragraph and a size number, and after the second half of this sweep the per-locale loop inside them asserts nothing any locale can fail. What survives is the SIZE case (a family growing is still the moment somebody has to translate a new key), which is a different rule wearing the families table's clothes. Worth deciding what that table is for before the next feature adds a key to one.

### Two-form-agreement follow-ups (2026-08-22)

- **[measured] The suggestion that started this named `de` and `es` and never checked `en`, which had seven of the twenty-one** — the model behind it was "translations lag behind English", and it survived being written by a run that had just proved the opposite in Russian. Worth recording as a bias rather than a mistake: a defect found in the translated locales is evidence about the MECHANISM, and the base map is written by the same mechanism. The cheap habit is to run every locale scan over `en` too, first.
- **[inferred] Nothing checks that a locale uses the RIGHT helper for its language** — `pl` calling `plural` with two forms would pass every case in the agreement suite, and would be wrong at 2–4. Deliberately out of scope for a syntactic scan, and it is one table away: language → which function, asserted against the calls. The reason to wait is that the table would be the third place the six languages are enumerated.
- **[measured] Six of the sixteen count-bearing keys avoid agreement by putting the number after a colon or in brackets** — `Перамешчана: 5`, `Filter (3)`, `noch 5`, `Chats, ungelesen: 3`. Several were written that way by translators working around a map that could not express the rule. Now that it can, some would read better as sentences; it is a copy question, and the kind that only becomes askable after the mechanism exists.
- **[inferred] `galleryOpenPhotos` and `navChatsUnreadA11y` are screen-reader labels and were among the wrong ones** — a11y strings have no visual reviewer, so a defect in one survives every screenshot and every manual pass. `ru.syncingPillA11y` was found by a scan rather than by anybody reading it. Worth a sweep of its own: which a11y-only strings has nobody ever heard rendered?
- **[inferred] `plural` and `slavicPlural` both coerce and both silently accept a string, and the map always passes a number** — the tolerance exists because `TranslationParams` is `string | number`, which is a type that could be narrowed instead. If `count` were typed as `number` where it is read, both coercions would be dead code and the "falls to the plural for anything unparseable" cases would be testing a branch nothing can reach.

"" : "s"}` in `en`). `de.exportPdfItemCount` renders "1 Objekte" and `es.accessOpenFor` renders "1 personas tienen acceso"; both were written this week, by the same runs that were careful about it in Russian. - **[measured] Sixteen count-bearing keys, and the ones that are CORRECT are correct by avoiding the problem** — `Перамешчана: 5`, `Фільтры (3)`, `засталося 5`. Six of the sixteen put the number after a colon or in brackets, which is a translator's way around a rule the map could not express. The number it FIXED is `ru`'s, which was permanently short of a threshold for reasons no translator could act on.
- **[inferred] `TRANSLATION_FLOORS` is on declared keys and the report is now on translatable ones, so the two tables count different things** — deliberate (a floor catches a locale LOSING declarations, which is a fact about the file) and worth a second look the next time a floor is re-measured, because the notes quote percentages that are now computed against a different denominator than the one they were written from. Nothing is wrong today; the `ru` note was updated by hand, and the other five quote counts rather than ratios.
- **[measured] `filterSourcePlaceholder` and `wishlistSourcePlaceholder` name eBay in all six locales, which is the same class of key** — a brand inside a longer sentence rather than a whole string, so `UNTRANSLATABLE_KEYS` cannot hold it and should not try. But it is the same question the exemption answered ("is this string something a translator can act on?") arriving one level down, and it is still filed unanswered from three runs ago. One question to the product owner settles both keys.
- **[inferred] Nothing checks that an exempt key's VALUE is actually the same in every locale that declares it** — the exemption says "English is correct here", and a locale that declared `appName: "Коллекционки"` would be exempt from the denominator while shipping a different brand name. Cheap to check now that `ParsedObjectLiteral.values` exists: for each exempt key, every locale that declares it must declare the base value verbatim.
- **[measured] The two `searchFilterItems`/`searchResultsItems` keys are the inverse case and still open** — the same word declared twice in six locales because one labels a chip and the other a heading. Filed two runs ago. Where the exemption removed keys nobody can translate, this is a pair somebody translates twice; both are questions about what the denominator MEANS, and answering the second would shrink it by one honest key rather than by an exemption.

### Key-usage index follow-ups (2026-08-22)

- **[DONE 2026-08-22, six of seven] Seven suites ask the per-screen question with a rule this repo has already measured as wrong** — `share-sheet`, `bulk-bar-extraction`, `edit-collection-modal`, `move-collection-modal`, `collection-share-sheet`, `photo-lightbox-item-card` and `a11y-icon-labels` each build `new RegExp(\`t\\("${key}"\`)` against one file's text to assert a screen renders a key. That is `indexI18nKeyUsage(keys, [file])` with the `t("…")`-only rule the orphan guard abandoned because 43 of 502 base keys are never written inside a `t(...)` call. Nothing is red today — those screens all use the direct call — and the first one to move a key into a table (`labelKey: "…"`, the shape `lib/item-filters.ts` already uses) goes red while still rendering it. Seven call sites, one helper, and the rule stops being stated eight ways.
- **[DONE 2026-08-22] The index is built and no rule sits on it yet, which is the whole point and also the risk** — six suites now read it through `assertReadsKeys`, so it is no longer a module with a suite and no caller; the per-SCREEN coverage rule below is still unwritten, and that is the half this entry is still about. The consumer it was built for is the per-screen coverage family: pick the screen with the most keys still English in the four partial locales (`byFile` answers this in one pass now), translate that screen's set, and let the rule be "this screen's keys are complete in every locale" — which is the first i18n claim that matches what a user actually meets.
- **[inferred] `byFile` is keyed by path and a screen is not always one file** — `app/collection/[id].tsx` renders through `components/item-card.tsx`, `components/bulk-bar.tsx` and half a dozen more, so the keys a USER meets on that screen are the union of a file and its imports. The index answers the file question exactly, which is the right primitive; whoever writes the screen rule has to decide whether a screen is a file or a reachable set, and the second one needs an import graph the repo does not have. Worth deciding before the rule is written, because the two answers give different numbers for the same screen and only one of them matches the complaint ("this screen is half-translated").
- **[measured] The looseness now points at single files, where it used to be diluted across 264** — the position rule counts a key-shaped literal in a key POSITION as a read, so a file that writes `{ pathname: "collection" }` is credited with reading the key `collection` if one exists. Harmless for the orphan question (one false read among 264 files changes nothing unless it is the only one) and NOT harmless for a per-screen count, where one file's list is the entire answer. Nobody has measured how many such collisions the tree actually holds; the index makes that a one-loop question, and the answer decides whether the screen rule needs a tighter rule or just a note.
- **[inferred] `unreadI18nKeys` is a projection and `formatOrphanKeyReport` still takes a file COUNT** — the report says "nothing in 264 scanned file(s) reads this", which was all the flat set could support. The index knows which files were scanned and could say something sharper on a near miss: a key read by exactly one file, or one read only by `__tests__`, is a different finding from one read by nothing, and both are currently reported the same way (or not at all). Cheap once the caller holds the index rather than a number.

### Scan-root follow-ups (2026-08-21)

- **[measured] Nothing now forces a floor re-measure, which means nothing now notices a floor going slack** — that is the trade this work made and it is worth stating plainly. `below_floor` fires at a committed number; the tree grows; the number stays. `check-problem-phrasing-imports` is 535 against a walk of 716 today (25% slack) and will be 535 against 900 soon enough (41%), at which point a walk could lose two-fifths of its files with every root present and still pass. Nothing goes red for that, by design. `remeasure-floors` already computes `slackPercent` and already warns when it is too TIGHT; a symmetrical "this floor has drifted loose, suggest N" line is one `else if` and would make the slack direction visible without reintroducing a chore — it would be advice, not a failure.
- **[measured] `assertScannedRoots` and `assertScannedFloor` are two calls a wrapper has to remember to make in the right order** — six wrappers now carry both, roots first, each with a comment explaining why. That comment is the same six times, which is the shape the last four tasks have been undoing. A single `assertScannedWalk(CHECK_NAME, files)` that runs both in the right order would delete the ordering decision from six call sites and keep it in one; the two lower-level functions stay for the single-root guards that only want the count.
- **[inferred] `evaluateScannedRoots` reports the first empty root and stops, so a walk that lost three roots is three runs to diagnose** — deliberate, and matched to `scannedFloorFor`'s "raise the first problem" rule, but the two cases differ: an entry with three problems is one bad edit, while a walk missing three roots is usually one cause (a moved source directory) whose shape is only visible from the full list. Worth revisiting if it ever bites; the fix is a `roots: string[]` on the failure rather than a `root: string`, which is a wider change to the message table than it looks.
- **[measured] `FLOOR_WALKS` and `count.roots` are two tables naming the same roots, kept in step by one test** — `floor-walks.test.ts` asserts they agree, which is the right check, but the duplication is real: `FLOOR_WALKS` exists because the re-measure tool needs extensions too, and `count.roots` exists because the guard needs roots at runtime. Either `FLOOR_WALKS` should read its roots FROM `SCANNED_FLOORS` (leaving it to carry only `extensions`), or the extensions should move into the floor entry and `FLOOR_WALKS` should go. The second is cleaner and is a bigger diff; both beat two lists and a test.
- **[inferred] The `no_root_files` message names the wrapper's `SCANNED_DIRS` as a place to check, and nothing enforces that name** — the sentence says "spelled the same way in the wrapper's SCANNED_DIRS as in lib/scanned-floor.ts", which is good advice today because `guard-scan-dirs.test.ts` holds every wrapper to that one identifier. If that convention ever loosens, this message sends readers to a constant that may not exist under that name. Cheap fix: have the message name the guard's script path instead of the identifier inside it.

But `lib/analytics.ts` imports `lib/analytics-validate.ts`, which imports `ANALYTICS_EVENTS` outright, and every screen imports `lib/analytics.ts` for `trackEvent`. So the descriptions ship anyway, by the path the guard does not watch, and this task just added eleven value arrays to the same object. The fix is a build-time split (a `props`/`values`-only object for the runtime, descriptions for the doc generator), and the honest interim step is a comment on the guard saying what it does and does not achieve.

- **[measured] Nothing stops the twelfth value set being written as a plain array** — `closedSet<T>(Record<T, true>)` is what makes the tables exhaustive both ways, and it is a convention held up by whoever reads the file first. `UPSELL_SOURCE_VALUES` and `FRIEND_ACCEPT_DIRECTION_VALUES` already pass inline unions rather than named types, which is the halfway house a plain array is one step from. A guard is plausible here and cheap: an exported `*_VALUES` const in `lib/analytics-prop-values.ts` whose initializer is not a `closedSet(` call.

- **[inferred] `provider` is unconstrained and is the prop most likely to grow a bucket nobody expects** — it is whatever Supabase reports (`email`, `google`, `apple`, `unknown`), which is why it has no table. That also makes it the one prop where a silent new value is guaranteed eventually, and the dashboard is where it will be discovered. A `known-values` list that WARNS without failing — a third policy alongside throw and keep — would fit props sourced from outside the app, and `provider` is the only one today.

- **[measured] The dev throw is the enforcement and CI never runs in dev** — `assertValidProps` throws when `__DEV__` is true, and `npm test` runs under node with `__DEV__` unset, so the suites exercise the throw only by passing `failFast: true` explicitly. A call site that sends an out-of-set value is therefore caught by a developer running the app, not by CI. A source-level check (every `trackEvent("x", { k: "literal" })` with a literal value for a constrained prop) would move that to the gate; it would cover most call sites here, since most pass literals or typed unions.

- **[inferred] `listing_price_invalid.language` and `signup_completed.language` now declare a set the second one never sends** — signup fires with `{ method, provider }` only; `language` is in its `props` and has been since the taxonomy was written, and now has a value table too. Either the event is meant to carry the locale (in which case a call site is missing it and the funnel's locale slice is empty) or the key is vestigial. Ten minutes with `signupEventProps` settles it, and the answer decides whether to add the prop or delete it.

- **[measured] The marketplace listing cap is a premium gate that fires no analytics at all** — `overFreeCap` in `app/item/[id].tsx` disables the "list for sale" button once a free user has one active listing, and unlike the visibility chip it sends no `premium_upsell_shown`. Instrumenting it is not a one-liner, though, and that is the interesting part: the control is `disabled`, so there is no press to hang an event on. Either it stops being disabled and explains itself on tap (the pattern the visibility chip already settled on), or the event fires on render, which is a different metric wearing the same name.

A `AnalyticsEventPropValues` map for the small closed-set props would make the three of them checkable at the same place their names already are.

That is precisely the shape the last four tasks have been undoing. A `PRESSED_OPACITY` token, or a small `<TextButton>` that owns the hit-slop and the feedback together, would stop the third copy — and the third copy is what a "make the other text-buttons acknowledge presses" task would write.

That is defensible (there is no saved value to protect and the state starts from `defaultCollectionVisibilityForUser`), but it means the two screens now differ in whether the gate holds at the write boundary, and only one of them says why. Ten minutes to decide whether the create path wants the same belt-and-braces call, and either answer belongs in a comment next to `handleSave`.

- **[inferred] Nothing checks that a premium gate's UI lock and its write-time clamp agree, as a rule** — this task asserted it for one pair, by hand, with an exhaustive loop. The marketplace listing cap, the export gate and any future gate each have the same two halves and the same failure mode, and each will be checked by whoever remembers. A guard cannot see the pairing, but a shared shape could: a gate expressed as one object with `isLocked` and `clampOnSave` derived from a single predicate would make the agreement structural rather than tested.

### Seeded-suffix follow-ups (2026-08-21)

- **[measured] Nothing stops the wall clock coming back into a user-facing identifier** — the fix is three call sites passing `stableSuffix(user.id)`, and `wallClockSuffix` is still the DEFAULT of `slugifyProfileId`, `slugifyUsername` and both walks. A fourth call site written next month gets the 13-digit timestamp by omission, and the only thing that would catch it is a source-text case in `fallback-profile-locale` that names two specific expressions. The seventeenth guard writes itself: no call to a slug function inside `lib/social-context.tsx` (or any file that has a `user.id` in scope) may omit the suffix argument. Cheaper still: flip the defaults so the seed is required and the clock has to be asked for by name.

- **[measured] `buildFallbackProfile` still does not walk for uniqueness, and now the collision is deterministic rather than unlikely** — the standing entry said the creation path slugifies directly while only the EDIT path calls `ensureUniquePublicId`. That is unchanged, and the new suffix changes its character: two accounts whose names slugify identically used to be saved by the millisecond they were created in, and now collide identically on every device forever unless one of them edits their profile. The seeded suffix only applies when the name slugifies to NOTHING — two people both called "Ada Lovelace" still both get `ada-lovelace`. Whether that is a bug depends on whether public IDs must be unique at rest, which nothing in the repo states; that question is the actual task.

- **[measured] Six characters is a decision with no test naming its budget** — `SEEDED_SUFFIX_LENGTH` is 6 because 30 bits renders in exactly 6 base-36 characters, and the ~1.07e9 space gives a ~2% birthday collision at 10k anonymous accounts. Both numbers are in a doc comment. A case asserting the token length and the bit width TOGETHER would fail if somebody widened the mask to 32 bits (7 characters, `padStart` silently no-ops) instead of the length quietly changing under the regex that only checks `{6}`.

- **[inferred] The same shape exists in `lib/marketplace-context.tsx`** — `listing-${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}` mints a listing id. Not shared in a URL and not recomputed inside a memo, so neither half of today's bug applies, but it is the last place in the tree where an id is built from the clock and it is worth ten minutes to confirm the id is persisted at creation rather than re-derived. If it is ever re-derived, it is the same bug in a place where the symptom is a duplicated listing rather than a wandering profile URL.

- **[measured] `normalizeProfile` defaulting its suffix from `profile.id` makes an id-less profile's ID a constant** — `slugSuffixFromSeed("")` is a fixed token, so every profile with an empty `id` AND nothing to slugify converges on the same public ID. Unreachable today (the profile list dedupes on `id`, and a row without one never gets stored), which is exactly why it is worth a line somewhere: it is a plausible consequence of a future "draft profile" feature, and the failure mode is two strangers sharing an identifier rather than an error.

- **Three runs filed the same wrong claim, and nothing in the file marks a suggestion as unverified** — the `accessibilityViewIsModal` entry was written from JSX three times without anybody opening `node_modules/react-native-web` or asking what the sandwich was nested in. Every entry in `.suggestions.md` reads with the same confidence whether it was measured or inferred. A one-word convention — a leading `[measured]` / `[inferred]` on each entry — would let a future run know which ones need verifying BEFORE budgeting them, and this one would have cost ten minutes instead of being re-filed twice.

- **The sheet fingerprint is a prop count, and a shared `<SheetShell>` would make it a type** — the new suite finds sheets by "two `accessibilityRole="none"` in one file", which works because nothing else in this tree does that. It is still a coincidence being relied upon. The standing `<SheetShell>` extraction (nine hand-rolled copies of one backdrop-plus-card sandwich, each with its own style names) would replace the fingerprint with an import, make the Modal nesting structural rather than asserted, and give the accessibility decision one home instead of eleven.

That is a fact about a dependency at its current version, recorded in a doc comment, and an upgrade that changed it would leave eleven sheets relying on something that had quietly stopped being true. The repo already pins a dependency's behaviour this way for Sentry (`lint:sentry-version`). Whether the two always agree is unasserted, and a sheet whose Escape key does something other than its backdrop tap is a small, very confusing bug.

- **The suggestions file has never had an entry REMOVED for being wrong** — entries get struck through when done, and the wrong ones just sit there being re-read. This one is now marked, but the general shape stands: an entry that has been investigated and found not to apply is more valuable struck with its reason than deleted, and there is no convention for it. The three copies of this claim should collapse to one struck entry pointing at the suite.


### PII-guard follow-ups (2026-08-21)

- **The guard knows one PII field name and `lib/analytics-pii.ts` knows the whole vocabulary** — `check-profile-id-pii` hardcodes `email` because that is the field the bug used. The analytics layer already maintains a classifier over field names (`userEmail`, `chatMessage`, `display_name`) written for a different purpose. If its vocabulary is reusable outside analytics, the guard becomes "no PII field reaches a public identifier" rather than "no email does", and the next leak — a phone number, a real name column — is covered before it is written. The reason to check rather than assume: that module classifies ANALYTICS payload keys, which may not be the same namespace as profile fields.

- **The rule covers the assignment and not the function it calls** — `publicId: makeId(profile)` passes, whatever `makeId` does with the profile it was handed. That is the honest limit of a text scan and it is worth writing down beside the rule, because the obvious next leak is one indirection deeper. Closing it properly needs type information; a cheap middle step is to also flag a function whose NAME suggests it produces an identifier and whose body references `email`.

- **`displayName` is excluded by name and nothing states the invariant that makes the exclusion safe** — the reason it is safe is that a display name is not an identifier: it is not searched, not written into URLs, and the user can change it. Those three properties are what a reader needs to re-derive the decision, and they are currently in a doc comment on the scanner. If any of them stops being true — a "find people by display name" search, say — the exclusion silently becomes wrong. Worth pinning as an assertion about the app rather than a paragraph.

- **Sixteen guards now, and `lint:all` is the only place the list is legible** — the registry has a one-line description per guard, which is the right amount, and there is no page anywhere that says what the sixteen collectively protect. `docs/` has no guard index. A contributor deciding whether their change belongs in an existing guard currently reads `lib/lint-guards.ts` and guesses. Generating that page from `LINT_GUARDS` + `SCANNED_FLOORS` (name, what it forbids, what it walks, its floor and the note) would cost one script and stay true by construction — the `powerbi:schema-doc --check` pattern already in this repo.

- **The remediation query in MANUAL-TASKS.md has no expiry and no owner** — it is a read-only SELECT that will keep being true until somebody runs it, and nothing in the repo will ever remind them. The section is dated, which is the minimum; a line saying what to do once it HAS been run (delete the section, or mark it applied with the date and row count) would stop it becoming permanent furniture that everyone scrolls past.

### Locked-chip composed-key follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The visibility chip's ROW itself never announces the group** — a screen reader landing on the private/public choice hears two buttons with no framing, and one of them may be labelled with the new `visibilityPrivateLockedA11y` sentence with no cue that a "Public" option exists next to it. Wrapping the row in a `<View accessibilityRole="radiogroup" accessibilityLabel={t("visibilityLabel")}>` would give the pair a name, and the two chips would then be siblings inside a group instead of two independent buttons. The `radio` role for the children is the honest one — they are mutually exclusive — but it costs a per-platform check because `accessibilityRole="radio"` is in the type union but does not announce as a radio on Android before RN 0.75.

- **The upsell fires on the CHIP but not on the visible hint below it** — the same `visibilityPrivatePremiumOnly` sentence is rendered as body text under the row, and a sighted user reading that sentence and then tapping "Private" gets the upsell they were just warned about. A touch-target on the hint would let them ACT on the sentence they read — the same behaviour the chip has now, without the second-guess of pressing a chip that looks disabled — and would give the create screen a second entry into the upsell that costs no vertical space.

- **Neither chip is tested at runtime — both suites read source text only** — the new `visibility-chip-a11y.test.ts` and the two premium-gate suites all `readRepoFile` and match against regex. A render harness landing (the `[needs-dev-dep]` decision the analytics tasks are waiting on) would let the chip's spoken label be asserted against `props.accessibilityLabel` on the rendered node instead of against the string that produced it, which is the difference between "this file contains `t("visibilityPrivateLockedA11y")`" and "this button announces the premium constraint to a screen reader".

- **`visibilityPrivateLockedA11y` is the third key whose only purpose is to REPLACE what iOS speaks** — `navChatsUnreadA11y`, `galleryOpenPhotos` and now this one all exist because a `<Pressable>` with an `accessibilityLabel` on iOS silences the subtree, so any dynamic text inside the button has to travel INTO the label. There is now a shape to follow (a composed sentence, one string per locale, named `*A11y`) and there is no rule saying what triggers writing one — the next dynamic-count-inside-a-button will get its own suggestion and the same decision, made twice. Worth a one-line convention beside `check-a11y-jsx`'s `no_role` rule.

- **`visibilityPrivate` still ships in English for pl/de/es** — the composed a11y label now translates, but the visible chip text still reads `t("visibilityPrivate")`, which pl/de/es inherit from `en`. So a Polish user sees "Private" on the chip and hears the composed Polish sentence via the label — the eye and the ear disagree in three of six locales. Small fix, four keys (`visibilityPrivate`, `visibilityPublic`, `visibilityPublicHint`, `visibilityPrivateHint`) times three locales, no code changes.

- **The composed sentence duplicates `visibilityPrivate` in every locale** — `visibilityPrivateLockedA11y` for `ru` reads "Приватная: приватные коллекции — премиум-функция." with the value name repeated as its own noun. That is a stylistic choice made six times and no rule ties them together; a locale whose "private" translation changes (say, adopting a formal register) would need `visibilityPrivateLockedA11y` updated in step, and nothing checks that. A test that asserts `visibilityPrivate`'s value appears somewhere inside `visibilityPrivateLockedA11y` for every locale would keep them aligned — and would fail loudly on the German "Privat" / "privat" case difference that this pass fixed by choosing lowercase for the second clause.
