- **Five rules now, and each of the last three had to run "add the rest of the props" over the same fixture file first** — the hiding fixtures got `${HIDDEN}`, the disabled fixtures got `accessibilityState`, and today the role fixtures got `accessibilityRole="button"`. Every one of those touched the label suite's cases too, because a bare `<Pressable>` there asserts one rule and trips the new one. A fixture builder — `pressable(props, body)` — would make the cases say what they mean instead of a stack of props that grew each rule.

- **`no_role` and `silent_disabled` are both about a `<Pressable>` that will not talk** — they now share `IS_INTERACTIVE` in the sense that both require `onPress`, and neither ever fires on a layout wrapper. That is one predicate written twice. It is also the answer to why the guard's four rules used to feel like four scanners: they were, until the tag walk was shared. Reusing the same shape for the two `<Pressable>`-specific rules is the small next step.

- **`app/people.tsx` and `app/profile/[id].tsx` both write the relationship-action buttons once per branch** — sixteen and ten Pressables respectively, all with the same style names and the same handlers, differing only in `ProfileRelationship`. A `<RelationshipActions relationship={...} />` component would collapse both, get its accessibility right by construction, and let a screen skip the six-way branch entirely.

- **The scratch-sweep script is committed in scratchpad only** — the tsx that counted roleless Pressables is `/tmp/.../scratchpad/role.ts`, which lives outside the repo and disappears with the container. Every one of this week's sweeps used a script that shape and none of them committed one. `remeasure-floors` is the precedent for a sweep tool that lives beside the guard it feeds; an `unswept-roles` script would let anyone reproduce the "0 of 194" number this task ends with.

- **The suggestions file is now 6 KB longer than it was this morning and none of it has been pruned** — the seven runs today filed 35 suggestions and consumed six. The remaining 29 are entirely accurate against a tree that has since moved. A weekly pass that reads each entry against the current code and removes the ones that no longer describe it would keep the file useful; without it, the ratio only gets worse.

### Detail-screen role follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **`app/profile/[id].tsx` writes the same four buttons five times** — add friend, remove friend, follow, unfollow, message, once per `ProfileRelationship` branch, which is why sixteen Pressables produced one decision. `lib/types.ts` already models the relationship as a union of five; a table from relationship to the actions it offers would collapse the branch and make the sixteenth button impossible to add without a row. The reason to be careful is that the branches are not quite symmetric (`request_received` offers two, `self` offers none).

- **The listing sheet is the tenth sheet sandwich and lives inside a screen** — `app/item/[id].tsx` renders its own backdrop and card rather than reaching for a shared shell, which is exactly why it was missed by a sweep that started in `components/`. Any `<SheetShell>` extraction has to look in `app/` too, and this one is the argument for doing it: a sheet in a 700-line screen is where the next one gets written by copy.

- **`accessibilityState={{ selected }}` shorthand hides which flag it reads** — both item-screen chips use the object shorthand because the local is called `selected`, so the assertion counts two identical strings and cannot tell the condition picker from the mode picker. That reads well and it means a chip whose local was renamed would silently drop out of the count while the other still satisfies it. Naming the flag at the call site costs four characters and makes the case specific.

- **62 left, and `app/people.tsx` has the most of them at 10** — the remaining two slices are the list-and-create screens (35) and everything else (24, now 27 after the recount). Nothing in them looks structurally new: rows, form controls, and one or two more sheet sandwiches. Worth doing back to back rather than as two runs, because the payoff is entirely at zero.

- **The suite is now eighteen files and one number each** — it was written as a temporary holding pen until the guard could replace it, and it has grown a table, three special-case describes and a count per file. It is doing real work and it is also the thing that has to be DELETED for the sweep to have finished properly. Worth a line at the top saying so, so the next author extends it rather than treating it as the permanent home.

### Disabled-state follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **Five accessibility rules now exist and every one was found by hand first** — unnamed buttons, English labels, one-sided hides, undecided icons, silent disabled states. Each was a sweep, then a fix, then a rule written once the count hit zero. That pattern works and it only ever finds what somebody thought to look for. The remaining known-unswept states are `accessibilityState`'s other keys — `checked`, `expanded`, `busy`, `selected` — and `selected` alone is already written three times by hand.

- **`accessibilityRole` is absent far more often than `accessibilityState` was** — the disabled sweep touched 29 Pressables and most of them still claim no role, so they announce as generic tappables rather than as buttons. Unlike `disabled` this is not purely mechanical (`imagebutton`, `checkbox`, `search` and `link` are all correct somewhere in this tree), which is why it is a sweep rather than a codemod — but the default for a `<Pressable onPress>` is `button` in almost every case, so the judgement is narrower than it looks.

- **The codemod inserted 29 identical props and no test asserts any single one** — the guard checks the property repo-wide, which is stronger than 29 cases, and it also means a reader of `components/bulk-bar.tsx` has nothing local telling them the state matters. The icon sweep chose the opposite trade (per-file cases with the REASON in the title). Neither is wrong; having both patterns in one suite without a stated rule for when to use which is what will confuse the next author.

- **`ANNOUNCES_DISABLED` reads `[^}]*` inside a nested object literal** — `accessibilityState={{ disabled: a }}` is matched by scanning to the first `}`, which is the inner one, and that works for every shape this tree writes. `accessibilityState={{ ...base, disabled: x }}` with a nested object before `disabled` would not match, and the finding would be a false positive on correct code. The tag walk next door already has a brace-depth scanner; this rule reaches for a regex instead.

- **Nothing checks that the guard's five rules are all reachable from the CLI** — each has fixture cases and `undecided_icon` and `silent_disabled` each got one planted-offender run by hand, recorded in a task entry and nowhere else. `lint-guard-invalid-floor.test.ts` exists precisely because a code with no red run through a wrapper is a code nobody has seen fire in anger. Three of the five are still in that state.

### Guard-rename follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The suggestion was filed three times before it was done and nothing tracked that** — each run read the suggestions file, saw the entry, and filed it again in slightly different words rather than acting on it. Three near-duplicate entries is the signal that a suggestion is ready and it is also invisible: nobody counts them. A promoted-from marker, or simply deleting the entry when re-filing it, would make the repetition legible.

- **`a11y-jsx` claims a scope wider than the file's rules** — the new name says "accessibility problems in JSX", and the file checks four specific ones. That is the right direction (it was named for one rule and is now named for a category) and it also sets an expectation the file does not meet: no colour contrast, no touch-target size, no heading order, none of which a text scan can do. Worth a sentence in the doc block listing what it deliberately does not check, next to the one about not understanding components.

- **Six places knew the guard's name and none of them is the guard** — the rename touched `LINT_GUARDS`, `SCANNED_FLOORS`, `FLOOR_WALKS`, two fixtures and a package script, all agreeing by convention that `CHECK_NAME` in the CLI matches. `lint-guards.test.ts` pins registry↔package.json parity and `guard-report-paths.test.ts` pins the report table, but nothing checks that a guard's own `CHECK_NAME` constant matches its registry entry — which is the string every one of the other five is keyed on.

- **`git mv` kept the history and the suggestion files still name the old path** — `.tasks/.tasks.md` and `.tasks/.suggestions.md` carry a dozen references to `check-a11y-icon-labels`, correctly, because they are records of what happened. That is right for entries about the past and wrong for the ones still open, and there is no way to tell which is which without reading each. Worth deciding whether open entries get updated on a rename or whether the rename note is expected to be found.

- **Fourteen guards and the registry description is the only prose most of them get** — this one's was a sentence about a single rule for a file with four, and it was wrong for eight hours because nothing reads registry descriptions. `lint-all`'s output prints names and timings, not descriptions. Printing the description on failure would give it a reader, which is the only thing that keeps prose honest.

### Undecided-icon guard follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The guard understands one element name and the codebase has three ways to draw an icon** — this was filed this morning against the label rules and `undecided_icon` inherits it whole: `<IconBadge>`, `<MyIcon />` and `{renderIcon()}` are invisible to a rule that looks for `<Ionicons`. The difference is that the rule now claims the tree is at ZERO undecided icons, which is only true of the icons it can see. Counting `<Pressable>` bodies containing no element the guard recognises would say how big that claim's blind spot is.

- **Four rules share one walk and the guard is still named `check-a11y-icon-labels`** — filed twice already today and now overdue: two of the four rules are not about labels and one is not about icons either. The rename costs an entry in five checked places. Every hour it waits, another entry points at the old name.

- **`HIDES_SUBTREE_BY` and `HIDDEN_BY` differ on one platform and look like a copy** — two of the three regexes are literally the same object reference, and the third differs by `"no"` versus `"no-hide-descendants"`. A reader tidying this file would merge them, and the merge would be silently wrong in the direction that matters: children of an `importantForAccessibility="no"` node would be treated as hidden when Android still announces them. There is a case for it now; a comment is not the same as a check that the two tables DIFFER.

- **The stack pops by name and JSX has components whose close tag it may never see** — an unmatched `</Name>` pops down to that name if it is open and is ignored otherwise, which is the forgiving choice for a file mid-edit. It is also the choice that makes a mismatched tree silently under-report: a missing `</View>` leaves everything after it inside a subtree that may be marked hidden. The scan reads files that typecheck in practice, so this is theory today; the honest version would report a structural finding rather than guessing.

- **Nothing tests the guard against a tree with a hidden ancestor that is not a `<View>`** — the ancestry cases all use `<View>`, and the real coverage case in `item-card.tsx` is a `<View>` too. React Native's `<Text>`, `<Pressable>` and `<ScrollView>` all accept the same props and none of them is exercised as an ancestor. The walk does not care about the name, which is exactly why nobody would notice if a future rule started to.

The sub-tasks that follow are not mechanical (they decide, and some of them add i18n keys), so this is less a suggestion to write a codemod than a note that the temptation will be there and should be resisted for the ones that need a judgement.

### Nav-badge announcement follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The profile tab's premium dot is the third silent badge and was left silent** — `premiumBadge` draws an amber dot under the profile icon and is the one badge in the bar that is not a `FriendsTabBadge`, so it did not travel through the mapping the other two now use. Announcing it is one key in six languages plus a second argument to `tabLabel`; the argument for pausing was that a boolean prop and a badge union are two different shapes and folding them together is a decision, not a copy. The argument against pausing is that "two of the three badges speak" is precisely the half-fix this repository keeps filing suggestions about.

- **The label REPLACES the tab name instead of extending it** — while a badge is up, the chats tab announces "Chats, unread: 3" and the friends tab "Friends, pending requests", which are whole sentences that happen to start with the tab's name in all six languages. Nothing enforces that they do: the plain name and the badged name are unrelated keys, so a translator could reword one and leave a tab that announces a different noun depending on whether anything is waiting. Composing the badged label from `t(plainKey)` plus a suffix would make the coupling structural, at the cost of a comma that not every language wants in the same place.

- **`accessibilityLiveRegion` is what would announce a message arriving** — the label is correct the next time the tab is focused, and a message that lands while the user is reading a collection changes the count silently. That is the difference between a label being accurate and a badge being useful, and it is a real decision rather than an oversight: a live region on a nav bar interrupts whatever is being read. Worth trying with VoiceOver on the chats tab alone before considering it for the friends dot.

- **Six locales now carry two more keys and four of them are still under half** — `be`, `pl`, `de` and `es` sit at 42%, 40%, 40% and 40% against 545, and every accessibility key added this week widened the denominator for all four. That is the right trade (a new key written in six languages beats one written in one) and it also means the published coverage number falls a little every time somebody does the right thing. A second number — coverage of the keys a screen reader speaks — would say something the aggregate cannot.

- **`navTabLabelSpec` is exhaustive over the badge union and the union is named for one tab** — `FriendsTabBadge` is the type of the chats badge, the friends badge and any future badged tab, and it is called `FriendsTabBadge` because it was written when one tab showed both. Its doc comment still explains the precedence rule ("unread wins over friend-request indicators") that `bottom-nav.tsx` no longer uses, because the two tabs now build their badges separately. Renaming it `NavTabBadge` and retiring `chooseFriendsTabBadge` — which nothing but its own tests calls — is a small pass that would stop the type reading as a leftover.

### Three-platform hide follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **Thirty-six of this tree's forty-four `<Ionicons>` carry neither a hide nor a label** — the rule that just grew a third platform governs the seven icons somebody already decided were decorative. The other thirty-six were never decided about: `app/_layout.tsx` has three, `app/create.tsx` five, and each is announced on all three platforms as whatever the glyph font resolves to. A guard cannot close this, because "decorative" is a judgement and a rule that demanded a hide on every icon would be wrong about the ones that carry meaning. What would help is a one-off inventory with a column for the decision, so the next person meets a list rather than forty-four call sites.

- **`aria-hidden` on a `<Text>` is dead weight on native and nothing says so** — React Native's `<View>` derives the two native props from it and `<Text>` does not, which is exactly why all seven sites write three props instead of one. On a `<View>`, writing all three is redundant rather than wrong, and the guard now demands it there too. Teaching the rule which elements derive the pair would let a `<View>` satisfy it with `aria-hidden` alone — at the cost of a scanner that has to know React Native's element table, which is the thing this file has so far refused to know.

- **The rule reads one tag and hiding is inherited** — `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` and iOS's `accessibilityElementsHidden` both hide a subtree, and `aria-hidden` hides one on the web, so a child inside an already-hidden parent needs nothing at all. The scanner walks tags, not a tree, so it would report that child as partially hidden if it carried one prop. This was already filed against the two-prop version and a third platform makes it likelier, not less: three props is three chances to write one out of habit on a node whose parent already covers it.

- **The bundle check that proved this worked is not a check** — `aria-hidden` appearing 17 times in `dist/` is what distinguishes "the prop is in the source" from "the prop reaches the browser", and it was run by hand once. Every assertion that survives is a source match, so a Metro or `@expo/vector-icons` change that dropped the prop on the way through would leave all of them green. `check-bundle-secrets` and `verify-bundle-inlining` already walk the export for exactly this reason; a third walk asserting the count matches the source count is the same shape.

- **Fourteen guards, and the one that grew a third rule is still named for its first** — `check-a11y-icon-labels` now covers unnamed icon buttons, untranslated labels and three-platform hiding, and the last of those is not about labels or icons. This was filed this morning against three rules and the third has since doubled in scope. The rename costs an entry in five places, every one of them checked by a suite, and the argument for doing it now is that the guard's name is what a contributor reads before deciding whether their change is in scope for it.

### Paired-prop follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **`half_hidden` fires on an element and cannot see the one wrapping it** — hiding a parent hides its subtree on iOS, and `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` does the same on Android, so a child inside an already-hidden parent needs nothing. The rule would report that child as half-hidden if it carried one prop, and report nothing if it carried neither. Nesting is what the props are actually about, and this scanner reads tags rather than a tree.

- **Three rules now share one walk and the guard is still named for the first** — `check-a11y-icon-labels` covers unnamed icon buttons, untranslated labels and one-sided hiding, which is "accessibility problems a text scan can see" rather than icon labels. Renaming costs an entry in five places (`LINT_GUARDS`, `SCANNED_FLOORS`, `FLOOR_WALKS`, the partial-root fixture, the planted-offender case) and every one of them is checked by a suite, so the rename is safe and boring — worth doing before a fourth rule makes the name actively misleading.

- **The `openTags` generator is a JSX parser in a lint module** — it handles brace depth, string literals, self-closing tags and member-expression names, which is enough for this repository's formatting and not enough for JSX in general (attribute comments, `{/* */}` between attributes, an unquoted `<` in text). `lib/js-tokens.ts` next door already knows about strings, comments and regex literals for the same reason. Two partial parsers of one language is the shape that ends with a third; folding this walk onto the tokeniser is the merge worth considering.

- **The guard's floor counts files, so a rule about elements is floored by the wrong noun** — 46 screen files is what stops a walk that lost a root from reporting green, and it says nothing about a scan that read 63 files and found no `<Pressable>` in any of them, which is what a JSX-parser regression would look like. Counting matched TAGS as well as files, and flooring that, is the shape `check-secrets` uses for candidates versus matches.

### Icon-guard follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The guard understands one element name and the codebase has three ways to draw an icon** — `<Ionicons>` is what it looks for, so a button whose child is `<IconBadge>`, `<MyIcon />` or `{renderIcon()}` is invisible to it. That is a deliberate floor on false positives (a wrapper could carry the label itself) and it is also the hole a new icon component walks straight through. Counting how many `<Pressable>` bodies contain NO element the guard recognises would say how big the hole is; today nobody knows whether it is two buttons or twenty.

- **`untranslated` fires on a string literal and says nothing about a template one** — `accessibilityLabel={`Delete ${name}`}` is English with a hole in it and passes, as does `accessibilityLabel={someEnglishConstant}`. The rule catches the shape the bug actually took and the next one may not take it. Widening to "the label expression contains no `t(`" is one line and would also flag legitimate pass-throughs like `accessibilityLabel={label}` in a leaf component — which is exactly what `<NavTab>` does, so the rule would need to know about props before it could be tightened.

- **Two floors now share one number by agreement rather than by construction** — `check-clarity-input-mask` and `check-a11y-icon-labels` both declare 46 over the identical `app` + `components` `.tsx` walk, and the notes say they move together. Nothing enforces that: raising one leaves the other behind silently, and `remeasure-floors` reports them as two rows. A floor that could say "same as check-clarity-input-mask" would make the coupling checkable; the argument against is a table where an entry's number is somewhere else.

- **The planted-offender case proves the guard fails and not that it fails HERE** — the fixture copies `app/` and `components/` into a scratch root and plants a button in it, so what is under test is the report's path base. The real tree is asserted only by the run being green, which is the same evidence a scanner that matched nothing at all would produce. The floor under the walk covers the "read nothing" case; what is missing is one run over the real tree with a known offender temporarily present, which is what the by-hand mutation check did and nothing records.

- **Fourteen guards and the aggregator still runs them in registry order, sequentially** — `lint:all` now spawns fourteen `tsx` processes back to back, and the CI step is nine seconds of mostly identical startup cost. Each guard is independent and most of them walk the same two directories; a fan-out with a shared walk, or simply `Promise.all` over the spawns, would cut it. Worth doing when it is a minute rather than nine seconds, and worth writing down now so the next guard's author knows the cost is linear.

### Icon-label follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **`accessibilityState={{ selected }}` is the right word for a tab and the role is `button`** — React Native has no `tab` role in the subset this app types against, so the bar announces six buttons of which one is "selected", rather than a tablist. That reads correctly on iOS and is a slight lie on web, where ARIA would want `role="tab"` inside a `role="tablist"`. Worth one pass with VoiceOver and NVDA before copying the pattern; the alternative costs a wrapper element the layout does not currently have.

- **The search tab is never `active`, on purpose, and now says so out loud** — `active: false` is hardcoded because the tab opens an overlay rather than navigating, so the highlight would stick. With `accessibilityState` derived from the same flag, a non-visual user is now told the search tab is not selected while the search overlay they just opened is on screen. Nobody decided that; it fell out of one flag doing two jobs.

- **Three of the six tab labels reuse keys written for page titles** — `searchTitle` is "Search", `marketplaceTitle` is "Marketplace", `chatsTitle` is "Chats", and they are the headings of the screens the tabs open, which is why they fit. They are also free to be reworded for their own screens ("Marketplace" becoming "Browse listings", say) and the tab label would follow silently. Dedicated `navX` keys would cost six entries in six locales and make the coupling a choice.

- **`photoMoveBack` and `photoMoveForward` describe the chevrons, not the outcome** — "back" and "forward" match the icons and the reading order, and what actually happens is that a photo swaps position with its neighbour, changing which one is the cover. For the first photo in the list that is the whole point and the label does not mention it. A position-aware label ("Move to position 2 of 5") is the shape that would say it, at the cost of a params function in six locales and a string that is longer than the button it names.

### Shape-seam follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **`shape` and `tone` are independent and only three of the four combinations exist** — `hard` + `block` is reachable, typechecks, and has never been rendered: a squarer filled-red button that still hugs its content because `alignSelf: "flex-start"` lives on the tone. Nobody decided that combination should look like that; it fell out of two props being orthogonal. Either a case should pin what it renders, or the pair should become one `variant` union of the three shapes that actually ship.

- **The block shape's numbers came from one screen and are named after none of them** — `RADIUS_CARD` with 18/16 padding is what `app/collection/[id].tsx` had, chosen to match the export and share buttons above it in the same stack. That relationship is the whole reason the shape exists and it is recorded in a comment inside the widget rather than anywhere the sibling buttons can see it. The day one of them is re-padded, the delete button underneath stops matching and nothing goes red.

- **The colour-free assertion on the shape entries greps for three substrings** — `color`, `SURFACE` and `border` (minus `borderRadius`) is a proxy for "this entry carries no paint", and it would miss `shadowColor`, an `opacity`, or a spread of some future constant that happens to be named otherwise. It caught the mistake worth catching and it is the kind of check that reads as stronger than it is; comparing the entry's key set against an allowed list of geometry properties would say the same thing without the guessing.

- **Three widgets now wear two surfaces and the merge question is still open** — `DESTRUCTIVE_ICON_SURFACE` and `SOFT_DESTRUCTIVE_SURFACE` differ on all three slots, invisibly, for no reason other than arrival order. That was filed four days ago as a cheap experiment (repoint one at the other, look at the wishlist row, keep or revert) and this change makes it cheaper still: with the last hand-written copy gone, every consumer of either trio is now a widget, so the experiment is a one-line edit in `lib/danger-surface.ts` and a look at two screens.

- **A widget adopted by a screen is pinned by a regex over that screen's JSX** — the new case matches `<DangerSection shape="block" actionLabel={t("deleteCollection")} onAction={handleDeleteCollection} />` down to the prop order, which is the fourth adoption case in this suite written that way and the fourth that a prettier reflow would redden. The suites cannot mount the component under `tsx --test`, so source matching is the only tool available; what would help is one helper that asserts "this file renders <X> with these props" without pinning their order.

### Required-key follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The list is audited against one screen and the rule is about every screen** — `REQUIRED_IN_EVERY_LOCALE` must name keys `app/settings.tsx` still renders, which is honest today because all four live in the language card and dishonest the moment a fifth key belongs somewhere else. The failure it would produce is the confusing kind: a key genuinely required everywhere, rendered by a screen that is not settings, reported as a stale entry to be dropped. Either the audit should sweep `app/` and `components/`, or the list should carry the screen each key belongs to and check that one.

- **A locale can declare a required key and paste the English string into it** — "declared" is the recorded decision that somebody looked at the key, which is the right measure for coverage and a weak one for exactly these four: the whole argument for the list is that an English `partial` badge under a German flag is self-defeating, and `languagePartial: "partial"` in the `de` map satisfies the rule while shipping precisely that. Value comparison is refused elsewhere for good reasons (`appName` is a brand, `emailPlaceholder` is an address), and none of those reasons apply to a four-key list where every entry is prose meant to be read in the reader's own language.

- **Nothing connects the list to the four languages it exists for** — `PARTIALLY_TRANSLATED_LANGUAGES` names `be`, `pl`, `de`, `es`, and the required-key rule applies to all six locales including `ru` at 99% and `en` itself. That is the simpler rule and it is not the rule the reasoning describes: two of the four keys are warnings addressed specifically to speakers of the partial languages. Worth deciding whether the list is "every locale" (today, cheap, slightly overbroad) or "every locale the badge can appear on" (what the argument actually says), because the two diverge the day a locale is finished.

- **`translationKeysUsed` is the third `t("key")` reader in this repository and the first one exported** — the analytics-i18n parity suite and the stale-placeholder suite each match the same call shape their own way. Three parsers of one call shape is the state `listSourceFiles` was in before seven guards were merged onto it, and this one is now the only one with a word boundary and a documented refusal to guess at computed keys. Merging the other two onto it is mechanical; the argument against is that each currently wants a slightly different shape of answer.

- **The reason-shape check greps for three words and calls it an argument** — an entry passes the bar by containing "fallback", "inherit" or "English" anywhere in its sentence, which is a proxy for "this reason is about what the fallback costs" and is satisfied by any sentence that mentions English at all. It caught two real cases on the way in, so it is not theatre; it is also the kind of check that trains the next writer to include the magic word rather than the argument. A reviewer reading four sentences is the real gate, and nothing records that one happened.

### Walk-premise follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The excuse is extension-wide and both reasons are about named files** — `.js` is excused because `scripts/serve-dist.js` is run by node and imports nothing from the app, `.mjs` because three loader stubs live under the suite tree. Neither sentence is a property of the extension, so `scripts/build-something.js` that DOES import from `lib/` inherits an excuse written for a different file, silently, and every floor over `scripts/` keeps counting without it. `unusedUncountedExcuses` catches the opposite drift (an excuse whose files left) and there is no check in the direction that matters more. Naming the files rather than the extensions would close it, at the cost of an excuse list that churns with every new script.

- **`MODULE_EXTENSIONS` lists four extensions this repository has never held, and only the excuses are audited** — `.jsx`, `.cjs`, `.mts` and `.cts` are there so the first one to arrive lands in a check rather than in nothing, which is the whole point, and it also means four eighths of the universe are untested against the real tree forever. The excuse table gets `unusedUncountedExcuses` precisely because an entry matching nothing is a claim nobody re-reads; the wider list gets no equivalent, and the argument that it should not is exactly the argument someone will make about the excuses next.

- **`count_mismatch` cannot fire from this repository and the suite cannot say so** — both walks take `NEVER_WALKED` from the same constant and the same `listFilesUnder`, so the only way the counts diverge is a caller passing its own skip list, which nothing does. The code is right, the fixture proves the arithmetic, and a reader meeting a branch with no reachable producer has no way to tell "belt and braces" from "left over". The tracked-`.local.` probe and the bundle walk have the same shape and the same silence; three of them is a pattern that wants one sentence somewhere central about branches kept for a caller that does not exist yet.

- **The premise walks every root twice and only one of its two callers memoises** — the suite caches per root because `app/` appears in four of the five walks and `__tests__/` is 431 files; `scripts/remeasure-floors.ts` re-tallies `app/` four times and `__tests__/` once per row that names it. It is a hand-run tool over a few hundred files, so the cost is invisible today and the asymmetry is real: the same walk is cheap in one caller by construction and cheap in the other by luck. Memoising inside `tallyExtensions` would make it neither.

- **`remeasure-floors` now exits 1 for two different reasons and still calls itself "not a guard"** — a moved floor is advice (re-measure, and write the note only a person can write); a walk that is not measuring what it declares is a defect with nothing optional about it. The second is exactly the shape `lint:all` exists for, and it is now computed by a script that CI never runs, so the property is enforced by `floor-walks.test.ts` alone. Splitting the exit statuses, or wiring only the premise half into `lint:all` as a thirteenth guard, would put the mandatory half where mandatory things live.

### Counted-property follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The counting case will go red on an ordinary test file, and the fix is a floor edit nobody warned the author about** — `__tests__/` sits at 430 against a floor of 450, so roughly four more suites reddens a case in `floor-walks.test.ts` for a contributor whose change had nothing to do with floors. That is the floor working, and it is also the third distinct suite that can fail this way. The message names `npm run remeasure-floors` and the suggested number, which is as far as a failing assertion can go; what would go further is a run that fails EARLY and loudly enough to be read as "raise a number", rather than as one red case among 5798.

- **`floor-walks.test.ts` now both mocks the arithmetic and measures the real tree, and the two halves want different things** — the pure cases exist precisely so the interesting shapes do not depend on today's counts, and the new case is entirely about today's counts. They read as one suite and age in opposite directions: the first half never needs touching, the second needs a floor bump every few weeks. Splitting the tree-measuring case into the suite that owns tree facts (`lint-guard-partial-root.test.ts`, which already spawns for four of the five) would put the churn where a reader expects it.

- **Three things now check the single-root property and the division of labour lives in a code comment** — the counting case, the spawning fixtures, and the script. The comment on the new case says which is which, and it is the only statement of it; `lib/floor-walks.ts`'s header describes the table, and `scripts/remeasure-floors.ts` calls itself "not a guard" without naming what is. One paragraph in the module both readers reach for would beat a comment inside one of the three consumers.

- **`listSourceFiles` is now called from a test, a script and eight guards, and only the guards are counted as callers anywhere** — `__tests__/source-files-helper.test.ts` audits which suites hand-roll a walk and exempts the ones that walk something else, but nothing tracks who uses the shared walk or with which extension set. That is fine while there is one implementation; it is exactly the bookkeeping that was missing when seven guards each had their own copy.

- **The premise assertion checks each root walked to something and not that it walked to the RIGHT something** — a root whose extension filter silently stopped matching (`.tsx` renamed, a new extension unlisted) still returns a positive count from the files it does match, so the case passes while measuring a fraction of the tree. The guards' own floors catch that one level down, which is the argument for leaving it; the counter-argument is that this case exists because those floors need re-measuring, so it inherits the same blind spot it is meant to watch.

### Remeasure-tool follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **`entryPatch` finds an entry by `indexOf` and a second table keyed alike silently steals it** — adding `FLOOR_WALKS` to `lib/scanned-floor.ts` made the fixture that breaks `check-inline-hex`'s floor patch the walk table instead, and it was caught only because the rewrite then matched nothing and the `assert.notEqual` fired. Moving the table to its own module fixes today's collision and not the class: any module the fixture patches can grow a second `  "name": {` at any time, and the next one may be patchable in a way that leaves a plausible-looking file. Anchoring the search on the table's declaration (`SCANNED_FLOORS = {`) rather than on the entry alone would make the fixture say which table it means.

- **`remeasure-floors` is not in `lint:ci`, so the property is enforced by a suite that spawns four guards** — the script computes the same verdict from a walk in milliseconds; the suite proves it by building temp trees and running the real binaries, which is stronger and costs seconds. Both are worth having and nothing says so: a reader finding two enforcements of one property has no way to know the script is the fast advisory and the suite is the proof. One sentence in either file, or the script's exit status wired into `lint:all` as a thirteenth guard, would settle which is which.

- **The suggested minimum encodes a slack the notes only mostly agree on** — `FLOOR_SLACK` is 0.25 and the header of `SCANNED_FLOORS` says "~30%", with individual notes landing between a quarter and a third. The tool picks the tighter reading so it never claims more room than the notes it imitates, which is defensible and is a number nobody decided. Either the header and the constant should say the same thing, or the constant should be a range the tool reports against rather than a single value it computes from.

- **`FLOOR_WALKS` covers the five multi-root walks and the other five count floors are unmeasured by anything** — `check-secrets` (whole tree), `check-env-inlining`, the two migration guards and the taxonomy floor have no root breakdown, so nothing can say whether their slack has eroded. Four of those genuinely have no roots to break down; `check-secrets` walks one tree and could report total-versus-floor without the per-root half. Worth deciding whether "measured" means the property or just the number, because the tool currently answers only for guards that have both.

- **The partial-root suite skips `check-problem-phrasing-imports` and the reason is a cost, not a principle** — its fixtures would each copy a 400-file `__tests__/` tree, so the five-root walk is asserted by the script and by nothing that spawns the guard. That is the largest floor in the table (450) and the one whose largest root is 96% of the way to it, so it is the entry most likely to move next and the only one with no run behind it. A single fixture that copies the smallest root rather than one per root would cost one spawn and cover the direction that matters.

### Partial-language follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The badge tells the reader a language is incomplete and not how incomplete** — `be` at 41% and `de` at 39% get the same word, and so would a locale at 85%. That is deliberate (a percentage in the picker commits the app to a number that moves every feature PR, which is exactly why the classification is what ships) and it also means the badge cannot distinguish "nearly there" from "barely started" the day the gap between the two groups narrows. The suite already fails if that gap drops below 20 points, which converts the problem into a decision rather than a surprise — but the decision itself (a second tier? the number after all? a link to the coverage report?) has nobody assigned to it.

- **`check-inline-hex`'s floor has now been re-measured three times for the same event** — a scan root drawing level with the number, twice by `lib/`. The floor is doing its job and the maintenance is manual archaeology every time: count the three roots, pick a number above the largest, rewrite a note. The suggestion filed against `check-inline-radius` a run ago asked for `npm run remeasure-floors` printing current counts beside declared minimums, and this is the second guard to want it. Two askers is usually where a script gets written.

- **A fixture hardcoded the value it mutates, and the protection that caught it cannot say WHY it drifted** — `lint-guard-invalid-floor.test.ts` spelled `minimum: 160` into the rewrite meant to break the table, and the run that raised the floor to 168 left the "broken" copy valid. `entryPatch`'s `assert.notEqual` did its job and named the drift, so this was a loud failure rather than a vacuous pass — the nine other `rewrite` entries in that file are covered by the same assertion and need no audit. What is missing is one step further: the message says "the anchor has drifted" and a reader still has to work out that a floor was re-measured three commits ago. The rewrite now reads its number from `SCANNED_FLOORS`, which is the general fix, and the other nine anchors are still literals that a rename would break the same way — `label: "source file"`, `inputs: [...]`, the note's date shape. Deriving each from the table it patches is mechanical; the argument against is that a fixture reading everything from the module under test can stop testing anything.

- **Two translation keys landed in six locales by hand and nothing checks that a seventh locale gets them** — the parity that exists is between the picker and the coverage table, not between a NEW key and the locales that must declare it. `languagePartial` is the first key whose whole purpose is to be shown to speakers of the four partial languages, so it inheriting from `en` would be self-defeating in a way no other key is. A small list of "keys that must be declared everywhere" — the picker's own strings, at minimum — would say that out loud.

- **The picker is the only surface that says a language is partial, and it is the one surface a reader has already left** — someone who switched to `de` three sessions ago sees an English-heavy app and no reminder of why. A one-line hint under a screen's title, or a dismissible note the first time an untranslated screen renders, would put the explanation where the confusion is; the argument against is that it needs a per-screen coverage signal the app does not have, only a per-language one.

### Bundle-walk follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **The same observation was filed five times and nothing noticed** — "the bundle guard does not say why it walks" appeared in five sections over two days, each time as a fresh discovery, because a suggestion file that only grows has no way to say "this one again". That is a signal worth reading: five independent filings is a reader failing to find something, and it is also five entries of budget spent restating one gap. A count, a merge step, or simply sorting a new section against the standing ones before appending would turn the repetition into the priority it actually is.

- **`bundle-walk-premise.test.ts` asserts a guard's PROSE, which is a new kind of test here** — two of its five cases match a sentence in `check-bundle-secrets.ts` and the name of the suite pinning it, so rewording the header turns a test red. That is deliberate (the whole change is about documentation that a change can break) and it is also the shape that ends with a comment nobody dares improve. The other three cases pin behaviour and would survive any rewording; whether the prose-matching pair earns its brittleness is a decision, not an oversight, and it is currently only in a commit message.

- **The `dist/`-is-ignored premise is asserted twice, in two vocabularies** — once as "git's listing holds no path under `dist/`" (a spawn) and once as "`.gitignore` matches `/^\/?dist\/?$/m`" (a regex over the file). The second is the reason for the first, and it is also the weaker statement: an ignore rule can be overridden by a later negation, a `.git/info/exclude`, or a global ignore file, none of which the regex sees. Keeping both is honest belt-and-braces; keeping only the spawn would be the true one, at the price of a case that says nothing outside a work tree.

- **The two-clause case pins an ORDER that the wrapper picks by array literal** — `[formatLocalOnlySkips(...), formatUnreadCandidates(...)]` decides which clause a reader meets first, and the case now asserts that order to the comma. Nothing says WHY skip-then-unread is the right order (a plausible argument: what a rule removed is policy the reader chose, what could not be read is news), so the next person to add a third clause has a pinned order and no principle to place theirs against.

- **The `.local.` clause is only reachable under git when the ignore file is not this repository's** — the new fixture has to pass an ignore string that deliberately does not cover `*.local.*`, because the real `.gitignore` drops such a file before the scan sees it. So the case proves the clause renders, and cannot prove it renders on any checkout of THIS repository, where it is reachable only through the walk fallback. That is the "belt and braces" the module documents, and the fixture is now the third place that fact is encoded — worth stating once where the other two can point at it.

### Unread-fail follow-ups (2026-08-20)

- **`formatUnreadCommitted` and `formatTrackedLocalOnly` are the same refusal with opposite advice** — both count files, indent the names one per line, and close with a git command that fixes them; they live in two modules and share every line but the verb. One says `git rm --cached` (this file should not be in git), the other `git checkout -- <path>` (this file should be in the working tree), and that opposition is the entire content. A shared `formatFileRefusal(headline, names, remedy)` would make the third refusal right by construction; the argument against is that the remedy line is the part that must NOT be shared, so the helper would abstract the boilerplate and leave the meaning at the call site — which is most of what a reader came to read.

- **The verdict lives in a table the second secret guard cannot reach** — `IRREGULAR_KINDS` now carries `unreadCommitted`, the boolean that decides fail-vs-pass, and only `check-secrets` consults it. `check-bundle-secrets` walks `dist/` and so never produces an `IrregularPath` at all, which is the same "listing asks git, walk answers itself" seam that keeps surfacing. The bundle guard's file still says nothing about why it walks, so a reader meeting the table has no way to know whether the bundle scan opted out or was never offered — one sentence beside `BUNDLE_SKIP_DIRS` is owed here too.

- **Fail beats pass-clause, and no case shows the two candidates side by side** — a checkout that BOTH holds a tracked symlink (benign, a pass-line clause) AND is missing a committed file (a refusal) now fails, and the symlink clause is never rendered because the run exits first. That precedence is correct and pinned by nothing: the missing-committed run case has no symlink in it, and the symlink case has no missing file. One fixture with both would state which one wins when a checkout is strange in two ways at once.

- **The missing-committed refusal fires before a single file is read** — same shape as the tracked-`.local.` probe that already exits early: a checkout missing a committed file never learns whether the REST of the tree was clean, so a developer mid-rebase gets two red runs where one would do (fix the checkout, then meet the actual leak). Collecting the incomplete-checkout refusal alongside the matches and deciding which a reader should see first is a five-line change nobody should make without that decision — and it is the same decision the tracked-probe follow-up is still holding.

- **`missing-from-worktree` sums a mid-checkout race with a committed-then-deleted file, and only one is a refusal worth failing over** — `lstat` throwing `ENOENT` means the working tree does not hold the path right now, which is a committed file gone AWOL (fail, correct) but also a file being written by a concurrent `git checkout` in another process (transient, and a re-run is green). The guard cannot tell them apart from one `lstat`, and treating the race as a hard failure is a choice made by the errno bucket rather than by anyone. A second `lstat` after a beat, or reading `git status`, would separate "gone" from "in flight" — at the cost of a guard that retries, which nothing else here does.

### Unread-clause follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **A committed file the working tree does not hold is REPORTED and still passes** — the run says `1 listed path(s) not read: notes.md (missing from the working tree)` and exits 0, which means a checkout that disagrees with its own index produces a green `no committed secrets` over a file nothing read. The floor exists for exactly this class of vacuous pass and counts CANDIDATES, so it is satisfied by the path that was never opened. Whether this should fail, or feed a second floor, is a decision nobody has made — it is currently the default that fell out of counting.

- **`formatUnreadCandidates` and `formatLocalOnlySkips` are the same function with different nouns** — count, sort, show five, `+N more`, empty at zero, and each has its own copy of the arithmetic. `LOCAL_ONLY_NAMES_SHOWN` and `UNREAD_NAMES_SHOWN` are the same 5 declared twice with the same paragraph. A shared `formatNamedCount(label, names)` would make the third one right by construction; the argument against is that the two live in different modules for a reason (one is the `.local.` convention, one is this scan's output) and merging them needs a home neither owns.

- **The `kind` strings are prose and they are compared as data** — `"not a regular file"` and `"missing from the working tree"` are a union in `scripts/guard-io.ts`, rendered verbatim into a report, and asserted by regex in two run suites. Rewording the message means touching a type, a formatter and four assertions, which is the shape that ends with a report nobody rewords. A code plus a rendering table (the way `SecretMatch` carries `ruleId` and `description` separately) would separate what happened from how it is said.

- **Nothing asserts the two clauses coexist on one line** — the local-only skip clause and the unread clause are appended by the same `map`, and each has runs proving it appears. A tree with a skipped `.local.` copy AND an unread symlink would put both on one pass line, in an order nobody chose, with two commas that have never been seen together. It is one fixture away and would pin the sentence a reader actually meets on a strange checkout.

- **`check-bundle-secrets` walks and therefore has no unread clause, which now reads as a gap rather than a decision** — the source scan says which set it read and what in that set it could not; the bundle scan says neither, because `listFilesUnder` answers both questions while it recurses and drops the answers. That is right and it is invisible: the third guard to take candidates from anywhere but a walk will have to rediscover why the first two differ.

### Regular-file follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`check-bundle-secrets` walks `dist/`, and a build could put a symlink in it** — the source scan now asks whether a candidate is a regular file; the bundle scan gets the answer for free from `listFilesUnder` and would lose it the day it took its candidates from anywhere else. That is the same silence `BUNDLE_SKIP_DIRS` exists to break: the guard's file says nothing about why walking is the right way to enumerate a generated directory, and now there are two properties riding on it rather than one.

- **The count says how many and the guard never says which** — `1 listed path(s) not regular files` on the pass line is enough to notice a change and not enough to act on one. A tracked symlink with a scanned extension is a genuinely odd thing for this repository to hold, and the run that first reports one gives its reader no name to look for. The skip clause next door names up to five and counts the rest; this could take the same shape, and the argument against is that it is normal-and-boring in repositories that use links for docs.

- **`partitionRegularFiles` stats every candidate, which is ~780 `lstat` calls on a clean run** — cheap next to reading all of them, and it is a second full pass over the candidate set on top of the second walk `notListed` already pays for. `git ls-files --stage` prints the mode (`120000` for a link) in the listing the guard already spawns, which would answer both questions in one process and without touching the disk — at the price of parsing a second git format, which is exactly the trade the `notListed` count declined.

- **A symlink is dropped and a file the index holds but the working tree lacks is dropped, under one number** — they are genuinely different events: one is a repository that uses links, the other is a checkout mid-race or an index that disagrees with the disk, and the second is worth more alarm than the pass line's parenthesis gives it. Splitting them means two counts or a named list; keeping them together means the day something strange happens it looks like the day somebody added a docs link.

- **`git ls-files` can list a path inside a submodule, and nothing here has an opinion about that** — a gitlink entry is a directory in the working tree, so it now lands in `irregular` and is counted, which is accidentally right. This repository has no submodules, so the behaviour is untested and unstated; a reader meeting the count for that reason would have nothing to read.

### NUL-listing follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`-z` and `namesFrom` are two halves of one contract held together by nobody** — the reader assumes a NUL-separated stdout and the flag lives at each call site, so the third helper that spawns `ls-files` is one forgotten flag away from re-introducing exactly the bug just fixed, silently, for as long as every tracked file is called something plain. An `lsFiles(cwd, extraArgs)` that appends `-z` itself and returns the parsed names would make the pairing structural; the argument against is that not every git subcommand spells the flag the same way, so the wrapper would be about `ls-files` specifically rather than about git.

- **`runGit` decodes stdout as UTF-8, and a filename is bytes** — `-z` stops git escaping the name, and then Node decodes it with `encoding: "utf8"`, so a path stored in some other encoding (a latin-1 name from an old checkout, a filesystem that never normalised) arrives as replacement characters and the refusal prints a name that still does not exist. `encoding: "buffer"` with an explicit decode is the honest shape. Nobody has met such a name here, which is the reason to decide whether this repository cares before a guard meets one.

- **`check-privacy-baseline-provenance.ts` has its own `git()` and splits `--name-only` on `\n`** — the same two defects, in a wrapper that predates `scripts/git-io.ts`: escaped names and a `.trim()`. It is harmless TODAY only because the answer is used to test membership of one fixed ASCII path, which is a property of the question and not of the code. Either that guard moves onto `runGit` (it wants a different failure policy — it exits rather than reporting a reason, deliberately) or the risk is written down where the split is.

- **Three guards now depend on git config defaults and none of them says so** — `core.quotePath` decides whether the escaping this change is about happens at all, `core.autocrlf` decides what a scan reads on Windows, `init.defaultBranch` was pinned inside `initGitRoot` for exactly this reason. Each is a knob whose non-default value changes a guard's answer, and the only place any of it is stated is a comment in a fixture helper. One paragraph in `scripts/git-io.ts` naming the assumptions, or a case asserting them, would turn a machine-specific pass into something a reader can check.

- **The refusal lists every name and the skip clause lists five** — `formatLocalOnlySkips` truncates at `LOCAL_ONLY_NAMES_SHOWN` with a `+N more`, and `formatTrackedLocalOnly` prints one line per file unbounded. Almost certainly right (a refusal names everything you must act on; a pass line should stay one line), and stated nowhere, so the next reader tidying the two formatters into a shape has no way to know one of the two behaviours is the decision.

### Conflicted-index follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **Two callers of `git ls-files` now deduplicate and nothing stops a third from forgetting** — the property is "any answer built from `ls-files` output is a SET", and it is enforced by two independent `new Set(...)` calls with a paragraph each. A shared reader in `scripts/git-io.ts` that splits, trims and dedups once would make the next helper right by construction; the argument against is that the two split on different characters (`\0` and `\n`) for reasons that are themselves load-bearing.

- **The dedup keeps the FIRST spelling and the three stages can differ in more than content** — `update-index` accepts a mode per stage, so a path that is a regular file on one side and a symlink on the other is a real conflict this fixture can now build and no case does. `check-secrets` would read whichever one the working tree holds, which is right, but the guard has never been pointed at an index whose stages disagree about what KIND of thing the path is.

- **`stageConflicted` leaves the working tree alone, which is correct and is the opposite of what a real merge does** — during an unresolved conflict git writes the merged file WITH markers into the working tree, so the bytes `check-secrets` reads in real life contain `<<<<<<<` around both versions of a credential. The scan would find it either way, and nothing has ever handed it that shape; the fixture can now, in one more line.

- **The refusal's count is asserted at one and the message is built for many** — `formatTrackedLocalOnly` sorts, numbers and lists, and every run that reaches it in this suite has exactly one file. The plural path (two tracked `.local.` files, the sort deciding the order) is exercised by unit cases over the formatter and by no run at all, which is the same split the `.local.` skip clause had before it got a spawned fixture.

- **A merge conflict is one of several index states the guard has still never seen** — a path deleted in the index but present on disk, an intent-to-add entry (`git add -N`), an assume-unchanged bit. Each is a plausible mid-work state, each changes what `ls-files` prints, and there is now a fixture vocabulary that could express them. Worth a decision about which of these the guard has an opinion on before adding a helper per state.

### Index-state follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`stage` and `forceAdd` differ by one line and the helper now has three list-shaped options** — `forceAdd`, `stage`, and the ignore string that is not a list at all. Each new state a fixture can express arrives as another optional array, and the next one (a file DELETED from the index, a merge conflict leaving a path at three stages) makes four. A single `commits: {path, state}[]` would say what the shape is instead of encoding it in which argument a caller picks; the reason not to do it today is that two callers do not justify a schema.

- **`git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD` is now spelled out twice in `git-io.test.ts` and neither call is the module under test** — it is the suite checking its own fixture, which is the right instinct and the wrong home: `initGitRoot` is what decides what lands in HEAD, so the assertion belongs to the helper. A `committedIn(root)` beside it, or the helper returning what it committed, would let a case say "this is the HEAD I asked for" without re-deriving it through a spawn the module has no opinion about.

- **A staged file is committable, and `check-secrets` is the only guard that acts on that** — `check-bundle-secrets` walks `dist/`, which is generated and ignored whole, so the question never reaches it; the three floors and the source-walk guards do not ask git at all. That is almost certainly correct and is written down nowhere, so the next guard that wants "what could be committed" has one worked example and no statement of when the question applies.

### Force-add follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **The equality case compares three numbers and calls that "the same set"** — identical file, entry and archive counts over two candidate sources is a strong signal and not the claim: two filters that each drop one different file agree on every count. Comparing the pass lines is all the guard's OUTPUT allows, because it prints what it read and never which files. A `--list` flag, or the counts broken down per extension, would let the case assert set equality instead of cardinality.

- **`GitFixtureError` is the third error class a fixture can throw and the only one with a name** — `makePartialRoot` throws bare `Error`s with a `makePartialRoot:` prefix, the tsx-resolution probe throws bare `Error`s with a `guard-fixture:` prefix, and this one is a class because a case wanted `instanceof`. Three prefixes and one class is the shape that ends with a fourth of each; either the prefix convention is the rule and this should drop back to it, or the class is, and the other two owe a rename.

### Fixture-helper follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`git-io.test.ts` now imports from `helpers/guard-fixture.ts`, which is a 1300-line module about spawning guards** — the git-fixture helper is the only thing it wants, and pulling the module in costs the suite everything else in it (a `createRequire`, a resolver, a memo map). A `helpers/git-fixture.ts` would be the honest split, and the reason not to do it today is that two homes for "what a scratch root is" is exactly the drift the change above just removed.

### Subject-count follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **The count is computed by walking the tree a second time, and the walk is now dead weight on the day git's listing is trusted** — every run inside a work tree pays a full traversal to produce one integer. Cheap today (a few hundred entries after the skip list) and exactly the kind of cost that is never revisited. `git status --porcelain --ignored` would answer the same question in the process this guard already spawns, at the price of parsing a second git format.

- **Zero is silent, so the clause appears for the first time on the run that introduces an ignore rule — and nobody will know whether it was zero before** — the count has no baseline anywhere. A number in `lib/scanned-floor.ts`'s neighbourhood (an expected maximum, asserted like the floor) would turn "this went up" from something a reader might notice into something a run states.

- **`formatScanSubject` is a third report vocabulary in `lib/secret-scan.ts` and the module is now three things** — the matcher, the scan's policy lists, and the wording of a guard's output. `formatSecretReport` was there first so the seam is old, but the module's own header still describes it as a pure matcher with no filesystem access, which is true and no longer the whole story.

- **The `.local.` documentation now explains where a rule is load-bearing, and nothing enforces the explanation** — the walk fallback is exercised by the fixture suites, but nothing asserts that the pass-line skip clause is reachable at all under the git listing, which is the claim the comment makes. A case that plants a force-added `.local.` file and asserts the tracked probe fires would pin the half that matters; the other half is pinned only by prose.

- **Three of the four run suites now init a git repo into a 584-file fixture root, and each pays its own copy** — `secret-scan-local-skip-run` and `secret-scan-subject-run` build four work trees between them, and the copy is the expensive part. A `makeGitRoot` beside `makePartialRoot`, memoised the way the archive fixtures already are, would make the git-mode cases cheap enough to add without thinking about it — which is the condition for them being added.

### Committable-set follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`check-bundle-secrets` walks `dist/`, which git ignores entirely, and now reads as the odd one out** — the source scan takes its candidates from git and names the set in its report; the bundle scan walks and says nothing about what it looked at. The right answer is almost certainly "keep walking, `dist/` is generated and untracked by design", and that answer is nowhere in the file. One sentence beside `BUNDLE_SKIP_DIRS`, which already exists to make exactly this kind of silence into a decision.

- **The `.local.` rule is now belt AND braces inside a work tree, and only braces outside one** — git's listing already drops ignored files, so `partitionLocalOnly` removes nothing on a normal checkout and the pass line's skip clause never appears there. It still fires in the walk fallback, which is where it is load-bearing. Nothing says this out loud, so the next reader finds a rule that appears to do nothing and a clause that appears unreachable — and the tracked probe, which is the one part that matters MORE under the git listing, looks like the same dead code.

- **`selectPaths` and `listFilesUnder` share their filters by convention, not by construction** — one applies them while recursing, the other over a list, and `git-io.test.ts` compares the two only over this repository's tracked files. A tree where they disagree (a skip-list directory reached through a symlink, a name with a backslash on Linux) would be found by nobody. A property-style case over a generated tree, or `listFilesUnder` implemented as walk-then-`selectPaths`, would make the agreement structural.

- **Nothing measures what the git listing dropped** — the change is justified by "a scratch file is not committable", and the run says nothing about how many candidates that removed. A count in the pass line (`779 from git's committable set, 4 working-tree files not in it`) would turn the claim into an observation, and would make a future ignore rule that quietly takes a real directory out of the scan visible on the run that introduced it.

- **Three suites now spawn `git init` into a 584-file fixture root** — `local-only`, `secret-scan-local-skip-run` and `secret-scan-subject-run` each build their own work tree by hand, with the same six lines of config and commit. The helper belongs next to `makePartialRoot`, which already owns what a scratch root IS; leaving it copied three times is how `NEVER_WALKED` started.

### Guard-asks-git follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`scripts/git-io.ts` exists now, and the scan that reads untracked files still reads them** — the suggestion this change came from had a sibling: the scan walks the working tree, so a scratch `notes.md` with a pasted key, an editor backup or a half-finished migration is read and reported and none of them is committable. `git ls-files` would fix the class rather than the one case, and the reason it still has not been done is unchanged (the scratch-root fixtures are not repositories and would all report `no_files`) — but the "ask git only inside a work tree, walk otherwise" shape now exists as working code with a reason string, so the remaining work is the fixture question alone.

- **The tracked check fails the run before anything has been scanned, which is the right order and the wrong report** — a tracked `.local.` file exits 1 with its own message and the reader never learns whether the rest of the tree was clean. For a guard whose failures are usually acted on one at a time that is fine; for one that runs in `lint:ci` behind three other legs it means two red runs where one would do. Collecting it alongside the matches and reporting both at the end is a five-line change nobody should make without deciding which failure a reader should see first.

- **`runGit` closes stdin and caps the call at ten seconds, and no test proves either** — the timeout is asserted nowhere and the `stdio: ["ignore", …]` is the difference between a guard that fails and a guard that hangs behind a credential helper on somebody's laptop. Both are the kind of protection that is silently removed by a later hand that sees no test naming it.

- **Two guard-side helper modules now sit in `scripts/` and only one of them is in the walk's own partition check** — `__tests__/source-files-helper.test.ts` audits top-level DIRECTORIES, so a new file under `scripts/` that is a library rather than a guard entry point is accounted for by nothing. `LINT_GUARDS` lists entry points; there is no list of the helpers they share, and the question "is this script a guard or a library?" is answered today by whether it happens to appear in a registry.

- **The pass line now carries three facts (count, skipped names, git's verdict) and is assembled by string concatenation at the call site** — every other report in this repository that grew past two facts got a formatter in `lib/` and a test that reads it. This one is still a template literal with a conditional comma in it, which is exactly the shape `formatSecretReport` replaced for the failure half.

### Local-only module follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **The bundle scan is the other reader of the working tree and it does not honour the convention** — `check-bundle-secrets` walks `dist/`, which is generated whole, so a `.local.` name cannot realistically appear there and the omission costs nothing today. What it costs is the reading: two scans sit beside each other, one filters on `isLocalOnlyPath` and the other does not mention it, and nothing says which of "not applicable" or "not thought about" is the reason. `BUNDLE_SKIP_DIRS` is empty and written out for exactly this argument; the same sentence is owed here.

- **`skippedLocal` is module-level mutable state in a guard that is otherwise a pure walk** — the wrapper accumulates into an array from inside a `filter` predicate, which works because `main()` runs once per process and would silently double-count the moment anything called it twice (a test that imports the wrapper, a future `--watch`). Threading the partition through the call — `partitionLocalOnly(files)` returning both halves — would make the guard's output a function of its input again, at the cost of two lines at each walk.

- **Five names shown, and the number lives in `lib/local-only.ts` where no report can disagree with it** — but `formatLocalOnlySkips` is the only caller, and the cap is a fact about a ONE-LINE report rather than about the convention. A second caller with more room (a CI summary, a `--verbose` run) would either re-use a cap it does not want or add a parameter nobody asked the first caller about. Worth deciding before the second caller exists.

- **The failure note names `queries-local.m` and `queries.local` as the near-misses, and those are guesses** — plausible ones, but the repository has never seen a real misnaming, so the two examples in the note are what somebody imagined a reader would type. If the instruction in `docs/powerbi/README.md` ever changes the file it points at, the examples in the note go stale silently: nothing ties the note's wording to the name the docs actually ask for.

- **A guard that skips by convention now says so; the four that skip by `SKIP_FILES` still do not** — `check-secrets` prints one number for what it read and, now, the `.local.` names it passed over, but `__tests__/secret-scan.test.ts` is removed from every run by the named-exemption list and no output mentions it. The argument that produced this change ("a reader cannot tell a skipped file from a scanned one") applies unchanged to the exemption that has been there longer, and the reason it was not done here is that a per-run line naming a permanent exemption is noise where naming a file the reader just created is news. That distinction is worth writing into the guard rather than into a commit message.

### Local-copy follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`*.local.*` is now a repository-wide rule and only `docs/powerbi/` knows about it** — every other place that asks for a credential on disk (`.env.example`, `MANUAL-TASKS.md`, the Supabase CLI notes) predates the convention and names its own scheme or none. One sentence in CLAUDE.md, or a short section in `.env.example`, would make `.local.` the answer to "where do I put the real value" everywhere instead of in one directory.

- **The two git-backed assertions are the only thing standing between the skip and a hole, and they run in the suite rather than in the guard** — `npm run lint:secrets` on its own will happily skip a force-added `.local.` file, because the check that nothing tracked matches lives in `secret-scan.test.ts`. Moving it into the guard (one `git ls-files` when a `.local.` file is skipped, and only then) would mean the rule cannot be subverted in a checkout where the suite was not run — at the cost of the guard spawning git, which it currently never does.
