The `.local.` convention fixes the one case somebody was told to create; reading `git ls-files` would fix the class, and the reason it has not been done is that the scratch-root fixtures (empty-root, partial-root, planted-archive) are not git repositories and would all report `no_files`. A guard that asks git only when it is inside a work tree, and walks otherwise, is the shape that satisfies both — worth writing down before someone tries the simple version.

- **`isLocalOnlyPath` is exported from `lib/secret-scan.ts` and is not about secrets** — it is a naming convention the whole repository now has, and the bundle scan, the census in the partition case and any future guard would all want the same answer. It sits in the secret module because that is where it was needed first, which is exactly how `NEVER_WALKED` ended up written out in two places before it moved to `lib/source-dirs.ts`.

- **Nothing tells a reader their `.local.` file is being skipped** — the guard prints one number for what it read and says nothing about what it passed over, so a developer who misnames the copy (`queries-local.m`, `queries.local`) gets a red run with no hint that the name is the problem. Naming skipped-by-convention files in the pass line, or only when the run fails, would turn a confusing failure into an obvious one.

### Planted-archive follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **The archive suite copies 584 files to clear a floor that is about text** — `assertScannedFloor` counts files and archives together, so proving anything about ONE archive means first satisfying a minimum measured over the whole tree. A second floor shape — a count of archive entries, or simply the existing count with archives excluded — would let the fixture be one `.pbit` and a handful of files, and would say something the current floor cannot: that a run which opened zero archives on a tree that holds one is a broken run, not a clean one.

- **`makePartialRoot` now takes `string | Buffer` and only one caller passes a Buffer** — the branch is one `Buffer.isBuffer` test and nothing asserts it wrote BYTES rather than a UTF-8 rendering of them. The failure is invisible in exactly the case it exists for: a zip written through a text encoding is still a file, still lands at the right path, and simply fails to be an archive, which the guard then reports as one it could not open. A case planting two bytes and reading them back would pin it.

- **The report says `archive!entry` and only a regex in one suite knows the `!` is a boundary** — `archiveEntryPath` builds it, `formatSecretReport` prints it, and nothing can take one apart. A reader (or a future skip list, or an editor integration) needs the inverse, and writing it as a `split` at the call site is how the two halves stop agreeing about what happens when an entry name itself contains a `!`.

- **`check-secrets` is the only guard whose report can name something that is not a path** — the coverage case in `guard-report-paths.test.ts` requires every `listSourceFiles` caller to be planted or exempted with a reason, and it has no equivalent for archive-opening guards, of which there is now exactly one. When `check-bundle-secrets` grows the same capability — a `.zip` under `dist/` is not far-fetched — nothing would notice it shipped without a planted case.

- **A guard that spawns per case is memoised by root, so a fixture reused across suites silently shares its runs** — `runGuardIn` keys on (guard, root) and the new suite leans on that deliberately. It is correct here and fragile in general: a case that mutates the scratch root between two runs gets the first run's output for both, with no symptom. Either the memo should key on the root's mtime, or `makePartialRoot` should return a token that says the tree is frozen.

### Archive-scan follow-ups (2026-08-19)

- **`ARCHIVE_SCAN_EXTENSIONS` is a one-entry allow-list with the same failure mode the extension list just had** — `.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.jar`, `.apk` and every other zip-shaped format would arrive unscanned, and the partition case only asks about extensions the tree holds TODAY. The scan now has a reader that can open any of them, so the question is whether the rule should be "these extensions" or "any file whose first four bytes are `PK\x03\x04`" — a magic-number test costs one 4-byte read per file and cannot be dodged by a rename, which is exactly how a credential-bearing archive would arrive.

- **The `.pbit` is opened, decoded and scanned, and nothing asserts the guard actually walks archives on a real tree** — the wrapper wiring is pinned by four regexes over its own source, which is the shape `SKIP_FILES` had before it moved into `lib/`. The planted-offender fixtures in `guard-report-paths.test.ts` are the mechanism that would say it for real: a scratch root holding one archive with a service_role JWT inside, asserting the guard exits 1 and prints a path a reader can join back — including the `!` and the entry name, which is the part of that report nothing has ever produced.

- **A decoded archive entry has no `secret-scan-ignore` escape hatch that anyone can use** — the marker works line by line on text somebody can edit, and nobody hand-edits a UTF-16 part inside a zip. A legitimate match in a generated archive (a sample key in a template's documentation page) would therefore be unsilenceable except by exempting the whole file, which is the tradeoff the exemption list was just measured down to one entry over. Worth deciding before it happens: an entry-level skip list keyed by `archive!entry`, or the explicit position that an archive match is always real.

- **`decodeZipEntryText` guesses UTF-8 for anything with no BOM, and a binary entry decodes to junk that is then scanned** — harmless today (junk matches no rule, and the one `.pbit` is seven small text parts), and quadratic-ish the day an archive carries a 40MB embedded image: eight regexes over a megabytes-long garbage string, per entry, per run. A cheap NUL-density or `isProbablyText` test before scanning would keep the cost proportional to the text actually in there.

- **`docs/powerbi/README.md` tells the reader to export a filled-in `.pbit` and says nothing about not committing it** — the guard now catches that mistake, which is the right order to do things in, but the instruction that produces it is still the instruction. One sentence pointing the export at an untracked filename (and a `.gitignore` line to match) would mean the mistake cannot be made rather than being caught after the fact — the same argument the `queries.local.m` suggestion above makes for the text file beside it.

Either the guard should widen to any `.match(/…/g)` whose length is compared to a literal, or its comment should say it is deliberately scoped to the locale case.

- **`bundle-smoke.test.ts` is exempted by filename, which is the weakest form of the exemption** — the reason is written down (its six counts privacy pages, not locales) and the mechanism is a string match on the file's name, so a rename silently drops the exemption and a genuinely offending case added to that file is never seen. Anchoring the exemption on the counted expression (`PRIVACY_PAGE_TARGETS.length`) rather than on the file would exempt the fact instead of the location.

### Numeric-literal follow-ups (2026-08-18)

- **The phantom-key bug says the scanner should decline numeric keys OUT LOUD, and it still declines them by silence** — `0x2f:` used to become a key named `x2f`; it now becomes nothing at all, which is correct and is indistinguishable from the literal not having that entry. The module's doc lists quoted and computed keys as deliberate omissions because both are compile errors against `TranslationMap`; a numeric key is the third member of that family and is not mentioned. Adding it to the list costs a line, and the case that pins the fix would then be pinning a documented stance rather than an implementation detail.

- **`NUMERIC_LITERAL` is permissive by design and nothing states the boundary it must not cross** — `1__0` and `1_` both match, deliberately, because a malformed literal is a compile error long before it reaches the scanner. But permissiveness has a limit that IS load-bearing: the pattern must never consume a character that begins the next token, or the scan resyncs one token late and the `/` rule reads the wrong `prev`. `1..toString()` is the shape that tests it (the first `.` belongs to the number, the second to the member access), and no case covers it. Worth one fixture rather than one more sentence of doc.

- **The three separator cases could be two if the strict pattern were derived once** — `shows, for every row…` builds `" +"` or `"\\n"` inline and the mutation case rebuilds the inline half a second time, so the strictness that the field exists to restore is written twice and can drift on one side. A tiny `rowPattern(word, separator)` helper beside the table, exported or not, would make the mutation case assert against the same regex the row check uses — which is the only way it genuinely proves what it claims.

- **`separator` describes the example and is read as describing the WORD** — the field's values are facts about a string in the table, but every case treats them as facts about the language (`"newline"` ⇒ the word ends a statement). Those coincide today because the newline set is asserted to be exactly the three statement-enders. If a fourth ASI row ever lands, the assertion listing the three by name is the thing that breaks, and the fix will be to widen the list rather than to notice that the field never meant what it was being read as. Naming the property in the type as "what the grammar permits" rather than "how the example is written" would keep the two from separating.

- **The unassertable-claims block names three and there is no rule for a fourth** — the note beside `DIVISION_FOLLOWS` is a good record and is also a list that grows by hand, which is the recall problem the keyword table escaped. There is no test that fails when a fourth such claim is added and not listed, and there cannot be one. What could exist is a convention — a `@grammar-claim` marker in the doc comment of each, and a case counting the markers against the block's own count — so the block goes stale loudly instead of quietly.


### Reserved-word-partition follow-ups (2026-08-17)

- **The partition is three structures in two files and only one of them is in `lib/`** — `REGEXP_FOLLOWS_KEYWORD` lives in `lib/i18n-source.ts`, while `RESERVED_WORDS` and `DIVIDES_AFTER` (the other half of the same partition, and the authority it is checked against) live in `__tests__/i18n-source.test.ts`. That is the right split while the audit is a test, but it means the module ships half a partition: a reader of the table cannot see what was deliberately excluded without opening a suite. If the standing suggestion to move the keyword rule to a `lib/js-scan.ts` is ever taken, the exclusion record should travel with it as the module's own statement of scope, leaving the suite with the assertions rather than the data.

- **`CONTEXTUAL_KEYWORDS` is eight words chosen by judgement, which is the recall problem one level down** — `RESERVED_WORDS` is a spec production and is exhaustive by construction; the contextual list is not derived from anything, and it has to exist because `of` is a table row and is not a reserved word. So the exhaustiveness case proves the two sides cover `RESERVED_WORDS ∪ CONTEXTUAL_KEYWORDS` and says nothing about whether that union is the language. Listing which productions were consulted (`for`-`of`, accessor property names, `import`/`export` clauses, class element modifiers) in the doc comment would at least make an omission reviewable instead of invisible — the same argument that made the reserved half exhaustive, applied to the half that cannot be.

- **The row-shape check now accepts any whitespace between the word and its regex, so a row can claim more than it has** — `break`, `continue` and `debugger` put their `/re/` on the NEXT LINE, which is why the assertion moved from `includes("word /")` to `\bword\s*/re/`. That loosening applies to every row: a `return` row rewritten with a line break would still pass, and the distinction that matters to the scanner (can the regex stand on the SAME line, i.e. is there a division to get wrong) is now unstated. A second field per row — the separator the example uses, or a boolean — would keep the two claims apart and would let the same-line rows be checked more strictly than they are.

- **The `.` in `DIVISION_FOLLOWS` rests on an argument nothing executable can check** — the trailing-dot fix is justified by "a `.` cannot be the token before a `/` in any valid program", which is true and is a claim about the GRAMMAR, not about this scanner. It cannot be turned into a case: the counter-example (`p./re/`) is a syntax error, so it cannot be written in a fixture that compiles, and the scanner would happily read it either way. The doc comment is the only place the argument lives. Worth naming as a class of claim this file now has three of (this one, the ASI rows, and the newline bound on `skipRegExpLiteral`) — each load-bearing, each unassertable.

- **`consumed()` is documented as one call per token and the loop tail calls it per CHARACTER** — the identifier and punctuator branches record whole tokens, but the fallthrough at the bottom (`if (!/\s/.test(ch)) consumed(ch)`) fires for every other non-whitespace character, so a number like `1_000n` is six calls, an operator like `===` is three. Harmless, because only the last character survives and the word is cleared either way — and it is why the scanner has no numeric-literal branch at all and still divides correctly after every numeric form. But "one call per token" is now the invariant a reader is asked to hold while the busiest call site does not obey it; either the tail deserves a note or the numeric forms deserve a branch that makes the claim true.

### Keyword-rule follow-ups (2026-08-17)

- **`REGEXP_FOLLOWS_KEYWORD` has fourteen entries and one is exercised** — `return` is the row a case covers; the other thirteen were written from memory of where a regex may follow a word. `of` and `in` are the interesting ones (both appear in `for (const x of …)`, neither can precede a regex there) and `instanceof` cannot precede one at all. A case per keyword is thirteen lines of fixture for a file that holds none of them; naming the source — ECMA-262's `RegularExpressionLiteral` lookahead restrictions — would at least let the next reader check the list against something.

- **The scan now carries two variables that must be cleared together and are cleared in eleven places** — `prev` and `prevWord` are set in every branch, and a new branch that forgets `prevWord = ""` leaves a stale keyword one token too long: `return "x" / 2` would open a regex. That is one added branch away, and the fix that removes the hazard rather than documenting it is a single `advance(ch, word)` helper the branches call instead of assigning both by hand.

Both are right and both are accidents of one `if (!/\s/.test(ch))`. - **`collectElements` makes the scan's return type lie for object literals** — `ScanResult.elements` is `readonly string[]` for both closers and is now always empty for `}`, so a future caller reading `elements` off an object scan gets a silent empty list rather than a type error. Splitting the result (or making `elements` optional and undefined for objects) would say which scans can answer.

That is the parity net working, and it means adding a seventh language means editing three tables to make three suites go green — the point at which a run stops asking whether the tables should be one.

### Second-statement follow-ups (2026-08-16)

- **The two derivations of "nearest" agree on every root the case tries and share the one assumption that could make both wrong** — `nearestChainLink` climbs out of a `node_modules` and `nodeModulesChain` skips one, and both spell the test as `path.basename(dir) === "node_modules"`. A checkout under a directory genuinely NAMED `node_modules` that is not one (rare, and pnpm's store layouts get close) is skipped by both, so the comparison stays green while both answers are wrong together. Nothing here can distinguish them; what would help is naming the shared test — `isNodeModulesDir(dir)` — so the assumption has one home rather than two spellings that look independent.

- **The platform premise is pinned for the platform the suite happens to run on** — `path.basename(FS_ROOT)` is `""` on the CI container's Linux, and the claim in both doc comments is about "every platform node runs on": Windows drive roots (`C:\`), UNC roots (`\\server\share\`) and POSIX all have to hold. `path.win32` and `path.posix` are importable and need no filesystem, so the case could assert the premise on both namespaces instead of on whichever one the runner booted with.

- **`probeNearestLink` calls `nearestChainLink` and `probeChainLink` and the walk calls `nodeModulesChain` and `probeChainLink`, so the two ends of the clause now share no code at all** — that is the independence the comparison wanted for the PATH and it is not what anyone wants for the PROBE: a `ProbedLink` built two ways can differ in which path it keeps (asked-about versus resolved) with no case comparing the two. One constructor taking a path, or a case that runs both against a single planted root and deep-equals the results, would close the half that should not be independent.

- **Three cases now assert against `path.join("/a", "node_modules")` and friends, which are absolute POSIX paths written as literals in a suite that also runs `path.win32`-relevant claims** — they work because `path.join` normalises the separators and `/a` is a valid Windows-relative-to-current-drive path, which is a coincidence rather than a plan. Deriving the fake roots from `FS_ROOT` (`path.join(FS_ROOT, "a")`) would make them roots on every platform instead of on this one.

### Trailing-rest follow-ups (2026-08-16)

- **`ChainLinks` guarantees the LAST entry and every reader uses the FIRST** — `readonly [...string[], string]` is the honest shape of the construction argument and it defends the end nobody reads: a walk that stopped pushing the nearest link, or one whose loop never ran, would still satisfy it. The compiler now catches a dropped root link and would not catch a dropped `below.push`. A type that guaranteed both ends (`readonly [string, ...string[], string]` for chains of two or more, with the one-link root case named separately) or a case asserting the first entry is the resolved root's own link would cover the half the readers actually depend on.

- **The loop now stops one directory short of the filesystem root, so "is this dir a `node_modules`" is never asked about that root** — it is skipped on the grounds that its basename is `""`, which is the argument for appending unconditionally, and it means the two halves of the walk apply different rules to different directories. Correct on every platform node runs on and worth a case that pins the premise rather than the conclusion: `path.basename(path.parse(cwd).root)` is `""`, on Windows drive roots and UNC roots too.

- **`nodeModulesChain` allocates a fresh list on every call and five of its readers want one entry** — `nearestChainLink`, `probeNearestLink` and the refusal paths each walk from a scratch root to the filesystem root and discard all but the first link. Naming what depends on it in the case's own comment — or asserting the chain is strictly ancestor-ordered, which implies distinctness and is what the readers actually use — would keep it tied to something.

- **Three `describe` blocks now build `path.parse(path.resolve("/")).root` for themselves** — the filesystem root is the fixture that needs no plant and it is computed once per block, with `rootLink` derived in one of them and re-derived inline in the others. ### Chain-invariant follow-ups (2026-08-16)

- **The non-empty tuple is enforced by a throw whose branch nothing can reach, which is the shape just deleted three times over** — `nodeModulesChain` destructures its own list and refuses an empty one with a sentence no reader will ever see, on the grounds that a cast would let a future edit hand every caller an undefined nearest link. That reasoning is sound and the result is still an untestable branch in a file whose whole argument is that untestable branches rot. Building the chain so the root's link is appended LAST — the ancestors collected on the way up, the filesystem root's link added after the loop — would make non-emptiness structural, with no branch and no cast.

- **`nearestChainLink` walks the entire chain to the filesystem root and returns its first entry** — the nearest link is `path.join(path.resolve(root), "node_modules")` for every root that is not itself a `node_modules`, and the walk that computes the other N-1 entries is thrown away. It costs nothing today (one caller, on a refusal path) and it is the kind of thing that gets called from a loop later. More to the point, a direct definition would be a SECOND statement of the rule that could be checked against the chain's first entry, which is stronger than the current arrangement where the name and the value are the same expression.

- **The walk reuses the nearest probe by comparing `dir === nearestPath`, a string comparison standing in for "this is the first iteration"** — it is correct because the chain has no duplicates, which is true and is stated nowhere and is exactly the property a future de-duplication or normalisation pass would be added to guarantee. `chain.entries()` and an index test would say what is meant; a case pinning that the chain never repeats a link would defend what is currently assumed.

One constructor used by both, or a case that runs both against one planted root and compares, would tie them.

- **`ChainLinks` is a `readonly` tuple and the walk copies it into a mutable array to build it, so the immutability stops at the return** — every current reader only iterates, which is why nothing has noticed. The value is that a reader who wants to sort or filter has to copy first, and the type says so; the gap is that `[nearest, ...rest]` rebuilds the list one entry at a time for the sole purpose of persuading the compiler, which is a cost paid on every refusal path and every call in the new cases.

### Errno-reporting follow-ups (2026-08-15)

- **The unreadable-link refusal is decided by `unreadable.length > 0`, so ONE unrelated bad link anywhere up the chain hides the global-folder finding** — the walk goes to the filesystem root, so a stale `/tmp/node_modules` symlink cycle (or an `EACCES` on a directory in someone's home) planted by anything at all makes every genuinely-global resolution report "could not be decided" instead of naming GLOBAL_FOLDERS. Reporting only the links that could plausibly have CONTAINED the resolved path — or naming both findings in one sentence when both apply — would stop an unrelated link two directories from the root from suppressing the diagnosis the reader needs.

### Containment-check follow-ups (2026-08-15)

- **The provenance check is a pure function of two paths and is not exported, so its table has to be written through a process spawn** — every case that pins it (`NODE_PATH`, the symlinked install, the hoisted ancestor, the unloadable entry) costs a scratch tree and, for two of them, a full node + tsx boot. Exporting `resolvedFromCheckout` would let the interesting rows — a chain link that is a file rather than a directory, a resolved path that is a PREFIX-sibling (`…/node_modules_old/tsx`), an ancestor at the filesystem root — be a table with no filesystem at all, leaving the spawns for the one end-to-end claim.

- **`isUnder` is a string comparison and the resolved path's case is the filesystem's business** — on a case-insensitive volume (macOS's default, Windows) a chain of `/Users/me/Repo/node_modules` and a resolution of `/Users/me/repo/node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs` do not share a prefix, and the check refuses an install that is plainly the checkout's own. `fs.realpathSync.native` normalises case on those platforms where plain `realpathSync` does not; using it (or comparing case-insensitively when `process.platform` says so) would keep the refusal for the case it was written for.

- **Every case in this suite builds its scratch trees by hand, and the fake global package is now written twice** — `mkdirSync` + a `package.json` + an `index.js`, spelled out in two cases that differ only in what else is on the chain. A `plantPackage(dir, name)` helper in `helpers/guard-fixture.ts` would let the next case say what it is testing (an empty entry, a broken symlink, a manifest with no `main`) instead of restating how a package is shaped.

### Provenance-check follow-ups (2026-08-15)

- **`nodeModulesChain` walks to the filesystem root, so `/tmp/node_modules` counts as a checkout's own install** — the chain is every ancestor, which is what node walks, but "the checkout owns this install" is a narrower claim than "some ancestor could have provided it": a scratch root under `/tmp` accepts a world-writable `/tmp/node_modules`, and a checkout under `$HOME` accepts one in the home directory, which is a global folder by every meaning except node's. Bounding the walk at the nearest enclosing `package.json` — or at the git root — would match what a reader takes the sentence to mean.

- **The global-folder case pays a full node + tsx boot to test one environment variable** — it is the only spawn in this suite that is not a guard run, and it exists because `NODE_PATH` is read once at startup. The rule it proves (`resolvedFromCheckout`) is a pure function of two paths and is not exported, so the cheap table-driven test of the same rule cannot be written. Exporting the predicate and giving it a handful of synthetic paths would move most of the coverage off the spawn and leave the child for the single end-to-end claim.

- **The hoisted-install case creates a temp directory inside the repository, and cleans it up in a `finally` that a crash outruns** — every guard floor is a count over this tree, so a `guard-fixture-nested-*` left behind is a directory the next `lint:all` walks and the next `npm ci` never removes. A `finally` covers a failed assertion and not a killed process, which is exactly how the run that matters ends. Registering the cleanup with the runner (`t.after`) or sweeping stale `guard-fixture-nested-*` roots in the suite's `after` would make the removal survive the failure it is most likely to follow.

- **Both loader refusals end with "Run `npm ci`" and only one of them is fixed by it** — a checkout resolving through `$NODE_PATH` may have a perfectly good install behind it and a stale environment variable in front, and running `npm ci` again changes nothing. The message names the GLOBAL_FOLDERS rule but not the value that triggered it, so the reader has to guess which global folder answered. Printing `process.env.NODE_PATH` (and the resolved file's nearest `node_modules`) would turn the diagnosis into the fix.

### Loader-resolution follow-ups (2026-08-15)

- **The check resolves for the CJS condition and the spawn loads the ESM one** — `require.resolve` answered `node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs` on this checkout, but `--import tsx` goes through the package's `import` condition, and nothing says the two entry points must both exist. A package that shipped only a `require` entry would pass the check and fail the spawn with the empty-pipes signature the check exists to prevent, one door over. `import.meta.resolve` (or a one-line child process doing the real `--import`) would test the path actually taken.

- **Thirteen guards are spawned per suite and the loader is resolved thirteen times** — `tsxLoader()` runs before every memo miss, so a resolution that is the same answer every time is paid once per guard per file. It is cheap (`require.resolve` caches internally) and it is also the one call whose failure must be seen EARLY rather than on whichever guard happens to run first; memoising it per root with the failure re-thrown would keep the diagnosis and drop the repeat.

- **The bin-spawn sweep reads `__tests__/*.test.ts` and the helpers are where a spawn would actually be written** — the drift guard walks one directory level, so `__tests__/helpers/` is outside it, and a private spawn added to a helper (which is exactly where the last one lived before it was migrated) would not be seen. Widening the walk to the helper directory, or expressing the rule as a `LINT_GUARDS` entry over the whole test tree the way `check-analytics-imports` does, would put the rule where it applies rather than where it was written.

- **`stripComments` is imported from `lib/env-inlining.ts` by a suite that has nothing to do with env inlining** — the function is a general lexer and its home is a guard's private module, so the third caller will either import it from an unrelated guard again or write a fourth copy (`lib/check-problem-phrasing-imports.ts` already reaches across for it the same way). Moving it to a `lib/source-text.ts` beside the other pure text helpers would give the two guards and this sweep one lexer with one set of string-literal edge cases to be right about.

### Fixture-refusal follow-ups (2026-08-14)

- **`tsxLoaderIn` takes a root and still hardcodes `node_modules/tsx` as the thing that proves an install** — the check is `existsSync` on a directory, so a half-written `node_modules` (an interrupted `npm ci`, a pruned store) passes it and the spawn fails anyway with the empty-pipes signature the check exists to prevent. Resolving the loader the way node will — `require.resolve("tsx", {paths: [root]})` — would test the thing the spawn actually depends on rather than a directory that shares its name.

- **The leak check reads `os.tmpdir()` by prefix, so two suites running concurrently would see each other's scratch roots** — `assertRefusesWithoutLeaking` diffs the set of `lint-guard-partial-*` directories around the throw, and node's test runner runs files in parallel processes. Today the diff is empty because the other suites create their roots outside the window, which is luck rather than isolation: a partial-root fixture built by a sibling file mid-assertion would be attributed to this one. Having `makePartialRoot` take an optional prefix, or recording created roots in a module-level set the helper exposes, would make the claim about THIS call rather than about the directory.

- **`runPatched` restores by rewriting pristine bytes and nothing checks the copy between suites** — the restore is now inside the `finally` where it belongs, but "restored" is still only ever asserted by the case that patched. A copy that drifted for any other reason (a guard that WRITES during a run — the generator-backed `--check` guards are one `--check` flag away from doing exactly that) would leave every later case in the file running against bytes nobody declared. A `verifyPristine()` on `SharedPatchedRepo`, called in the suite's `after`, would turn that from an assumption into a line.

- **`entryPatch`'s brace counter ignores braces inside strings, and `SCANNED_FLOORS` notes are prose** — the parser counts every `{` and `}` between the key and the close, including any that appear inside a `note:` string. No committed note contains one today, so the slice is right; a note that ever quoted a code snippet or a `${...}` would end the entry early and the rewrite would land in the wrong half — the exact failure the counter was written to prevent, arriving through the text it does not skip. A test that plants a braced note would say whether this matters before a note does.

- **Five suites now build their own `makeSharedPatchedRepo`, and each one costs a ~200-file copy** — this file makes a third. The per-case copy was already eliminated once by sharing within a suite; the same argument now applies across suites, and the restore discipline that would have to hold (a `finally` per run) already does. A module-scope copy in `helpers/` with reference counting would cut the fixture setup for the three slowest guard suites without changing a single assertion.

### Shared-fixture follow-ups (2026-08-14)

- **`entryPatch` is exported from a helper and nothing keeps a third copy from being written** — the two harnesses import it now, but the reason the duplicate appeared in the first place (a function declared inside a `*.test.ts` file cannot be imported by a sibling suite) applies to every other private fixture helper in those files: `guardFor`, the `runFor` shape, the control-run builder. A guard over `__tests__/*.test.ts` refusing a `function` declaration that also exists in `helpers/` — or simply a rule that fixture helpers live in `helpers/` — would state the convention the two files now follow by accident.

- **The helper hardcodes `lib/scanned-floor.ts` in its messages and takes the source as an argument** — `entryPatch` never opens a file, so `ENTRY_TABLE_MODULE` is a claim about which file the CALLER will apply it to. A caller that used it on a different table (there is nothing stopping one) would get a diagnostic naming a module its patch never touched. Passing the module name in, or deriving it from the patch key `runPatched` is already given, would make the message a fact about the run.

- **Both harnesses build a `runFor(code)` that memoises through `runPatched`'s label, and the labels are hand-namespaced** — `problem-${code}` in one file and `lookup-${code}` in the other, with the prefix as the only thing keeping two runs of the same guard apart if the two suites ever share a `SharedPatchedRepo`. They do not today (each file makes its own copy), which is exactly why nothing catches a collision. Deriving the label from the patch itself — a hash of the rewritten bytes — would make the memo key a fact about what ran.

- **Two harnesses now copy `lib/` + `scripts/` at ~200 files each, once per suite** — the shared copy was introduced to stop a per-CASE copy, and the same argument applies one level up now that a second file wants one. A module-scope copy shared across suites would need the restore discipline to hold across files (it already does, in a `finally`), and would halve the fixture setup for the two slowest guard suites.

- **`makeSharedPatchedRepo`'s marker injection is asserted per case, and the injection itself is untested** — every case checks the copy spoke, which is the right claim; nothing checks the OPPOSITE, that a repo built without the marker fails loudly rather than quietly making every provenance assertion vacuous. The constructor throws when `lib/scanned-floor.ts` is not among the copied entries, and no test exercises that throw — so the one guard protecting thirteen provenance assertions has never been seen to fire.

Both encode, per guard, which wrapper reads what and in which order it asserts. Neither reads the other's knowledge. A single `fixtureFacts(checkName)` derived from the table — its shape, its declared inputs, whether its count floor asserts before its input check — would let both files ask rather than remember, and would delete the standing "the fixtures encode assertion ORDER as a comment and nothing checks the comment" suggestion.

- **Ten wrapper runs of one module's validator take ~8s of the suite, and nine of them re-prove the plumbing** — every case pays a full loader boot to establish the same chain (guard starts → reads its entry → raises → prints one line). The variable part is the sentence, which is now pure. One wrapper run per SHAPE (count, inputs, delegation) plus a pure assertion per code would keep the end-to-end proof and drop most of the spawns; worth doing only if the file's wall clock starts mattering, and worth recording either way so the next reader knows the redundancy is deliberate.

### Ten-code harness follow-ups (2026-08-13)

- **A delegated entry is never read by any wrapper, so its declaration is inert at runtime** — `check-privacy-baseline-provenance` is the only real `delegatedTo` in the table, and its guard asserts its premise in `lib/privacy-baseline-provenance.ts` without ever calling `scannedFloorFor`. So `empty_delegation` and `delegation_with_shape` on THAT entry can never fire in production; the new harness produces them through `check-appstore-config` instead, which is honest but sidesteps the question. Either the delegated wrapper should call `scannedFloorFor(CHECK_NAME)` for its own sake — one line, and it would make the table's claim about that guard enforceable where it is made — or the table should say out loud that a delegated entry is validated only by the test suite, so the next reader does not assume a runtime check that is not there.

- **`validateScannedFloors(SCANNED_FLOORS)` runs in a test and never in a guard** — `scannedFloorFor` validates the ONE entry it returns, so a broken entry for a guard that happens not to run (or that delegates) is caught only by `scanned-floor.test.ts`. `lint:all` runs twelve guards and could validate the whole table once, at the front, for the cost of a single call — turning "the table is sound" from something CI asserts into something the tooling refuses to proceed without. Worth weighing against the argument for the status quo: a guard should fail for its own reasons, not for a sibling's.

- **The ten cases assert the DETAIL sentence by re-typing a fragment of it** — `says: /not a positive integer/` is a copy of a clause in `PROBLEM_DETAIL`, which is not exported, so the two drift independently and a reworded sentence turns into a failing assertion in a file that has nothing to do with the rewording. Exporting `PROBLEM_DETAIL` (or a `detailFor(code)` accessor) would let each case assert `output.includes(detailFor(code))` — a stronger claim than a fragment match, and one that moves with the sentence.

- **Nothing asserts that a rewrite introduces exactly ONE problem, though the whole file depends on it** — the comment says it and the `says` assertions imply it, but a rewrite that tripped two codes would assert about whichever `validateScannedFloorEntry` reports first and would look green until the validator's declaration order changed. The check is cheap and pure: build the patched entry object in-process, run `validateScannedFloorEntry` on it, and require exactly one problem whose code is the case's key. That is a unit assertion beside a wrapper assertion, and it pins the premise the wrapper run cannot see.

- **`entryPatch` finds the entry's end with `indexOf("\n  },", start)` and would silently mis-slice a nested object** — no entry in `SCANNED_FLOORS` nests today, so the first `\n  },` after the key really is the entry's close; the day one grows a nested shape, the slice ends early, the rewrite lands in the wrong half, and `runPatched`'s no-op check may not catch it because the patch did change SOMETHING. Counting braces from the opening one costs about six lines and makes the fixture's parse a fact rather than an assumption about the table's current formatting.

### Shared-copy harness follow-ups (2026-08-13)

- **Eight of ten `SCANNED_FLOORS` problem codes still have no wrapper run, and the copy that was blocking them is gone** — `validateScannedFloorEntry` reports ten ways an entry can be unusable and `lint-guard-invalid-floor.test.ts` runs two (`invalid_minimum`, `empty_inputs`). The reason to defer the rest was cost: one recursive copy per case. `runPatched` made a case two `writeFileSync` calls, so each remaining code is now a `patchedRun(label, from, to, checkName)` one-liner. `delegation_with_shape` is the one to run first — it is the only problem that means TWO places claim to own one premise, which is the exact shape that produces a guard everybody believes is covered.

- **Nothing asserts that the marker is on the copy's critical path rather than merely in the copy** — `makeSharedPatchedRepo` injects `console.error(PATCHED_REPO_MARKER)` into `lib/scanned-floor.ts` because every wrapper imports it, and that claim is load-bearing for every provenance assertion in the file. It is also a fact about twelve wrappers that nothing checks: a thirteenth guard that reached its premise some other way would print no marker, and its provenance assertion would fail with "the copy did not speak" when the truth is "this guard does not import the module the marker lives in". A registry-driven assertion — every `LINT_GUARDS` entry, run once out of a shared copy, must print the marker — would state the invariant where it is actually true.

- **`spawnSync` now captures stderr on green runs, and nothing yet reads it** — the channel was being discarded, which made "an ordinary run announces nothing about the override" vacuous; that one assertion is now real, and it is the only one. Every guard's PASS line, its premise note, and any warning it emits on the way to exiting 0 are newly visible to the harnesses and unexamined by them. The cheapest first use: assert that a guard exiting 0 prints NOTHING on stderr unless it was redirected — a guard that has started warning on every successful run is a thing the fleet should have to declare.

- **The empty-root suite is the last harness with its own idea of what a scan root is** — it was migrated onto the shared spawn but still builds its own `mkdtempSync` root and its own `after` cleanup, as do the partial-root, empty-input and invalid-floor files: four copies of the same six-line lifecycle, each leaking its roots if a fixture throws during construction rather than during a test. The standing `useScratchRoots()` suggestion now has one more caller and one fewer excuse; with the spawn already shared, the lifecycle is the only thing left that is four things.

- **`runPatched` re-applies and re-restores on a memo HIT, and the memo is the only reason that is cheap** — a cached run still walks the patch functions, rewrites the file, and writes the pristine bytes back before returning a result the spawn never produced. It is correct and it is a few KB of I/O per assertion, so it does not matter today; it matters the moment a patch function does something heavier than `String.replace`, or a fixture patches a file large enough for the write to be the cost. Checking the memo before applying — by exposing the key builder rather than duplicating it — makes the fast path actually fast and removes the only place where the fixture's behaviour depends on the cache being cheap.

### Restored-harness follow-ups (2026-08-13)

- **`tsxLoader()` proved to be dead code in the one situation it exists for, and nothing would have told us** — the check throws a sentence naming `npm ci`, and until this run that throw happened inside the `execFileSync` argument list, where the surrounding `catch` rewrote it into `{ output: "", status: 1 }` — the exact empty-output refusal it was written to distinguish itself from. The ordering is fixed; the fact that a checkout with no `node_modules` was the only thing that revealed it is the finding. A suite that stubs `TSX_MODULE` to a path that does not exist and asserts `runGuardFrom` THROWS (rather than returning a captured failure) would pin the property, and would catch the next well-meaning refactor that folds the call back into the try.

The lesson is procedural, but it has a mechanical form: a note in `CONTRIBUTING`/`CLAUDE.md` saying that a check run is only evidence when its OWN timestamps have advanced between two reads — never on a single snapshot, never on two identical ones — would make the next reader spend a second poll instead of a revert.

- **Nothing asserts the guard-fixture memo key covers `scriptRoot`, and the copied-repo split is what made that necessary** — `runGuardIn` and `runGuardFrom` now share one `runs` map, and correctness depends on `scriptRoot` being part of the key: without it, the control copy and a patched copy of the SAME guard against the SAME scan root collide, the second read returns the first's result, and a green control would certify a patch that never ran. It is right today and it is one dropped template field from being silently wrong forever, because the wrong answer is a cache hit rather than an error. A two-line test — same guard, two different `scriptRoot`s, assert the statuses differ — costs one extra copy and makes the invariant a thing that fails rather than a thing that is remembered.

- **The negative control asserts the copy RUNS; nothing asserts the copy is the thing that ran** — `runGuardFrom(guard, control.root, REPO_ROOT)` passing proves a wrapper executed and exited 0, but a bug that resolved `guard.scriptPath` against `REPO_ROOT` instead of `scriptRoot` would produce exactly the same green, and would make every patched fixture in the file silently run the committed table. The patched cases catch it today only because they expect a refusal — which means the whole file's integrity rests on the patches, not on the control. Having the control patch print a marker (a `console.error` line the copy emits and the real checkout cannot) would let the control assert provenance rather than mere success.

- **Two of ten `SCANNED_FLOORS` problem codes have a wrapper run, and the copies are now the cost driver** — this pairs with the standing "copy once, patch per case" suggestion and raises its priority: each of the eight remaining codes adds a full `lib/` + `scripts/` copy at ~200 files, so covering them at the current shape is 8 more copies before a single new assertion is written. Doing the shared-copy refactor FIRST turns the remaining eight into `patchedTable(from, to)` one-liners over one fixture, which is the difference between a cheap follow-up and one that doubles the suite's wall clock.

A `useScratchRoots()` helper in `guard-fixture.ts` returning a tracked factory would make the lifecycle one thing, and would give the leak-on-construction case one place to be fixed.

Both facts are derivable: the count floor is in the table, and the siblings are the other names in `inputs`. A fixture builder that took only the input to blank and read the rest from `SCANNED_FLOORS` would shrink the map to a list of names and delete the standing "the fixtures encode assertion ORDER as a comment and nothing checks the comment" suggestion along with it.

Gate the count floor on `checkOnly` and leave the input assertion unconditional.

- **`CHECK_NAME` is now duplicated in twelve scripts and pinned by a regex in the test** — the test greps `const CHECK_NAME = "..."` out of each wrapper as text and compares it to a key derived from `scriptPath`. It works, and it is a string-matching stand-in for something the registry could own outright: add `checkName` to the `LintGuard` interface, have each wrapper import its own name from `LINT_GUARDS`, and the parity becomes a type error instead of a test that reads source files as strings.

### Scanned-floor follow-ups (2026-08-12)

- **`evaluateScannedFiles` in `lib/bundle-premise.ts` is the same check with a weaker test, and it guards the bundle** — it fails only `count <= 0`, which is precisely the `no_files` half of the new floor; the `below_floor` half it lacks is the one that matters for `dist/`, where a partial export (Metro wrote one chunk before dying, a platform flag changed what got emitted) leaves a walk that finds SOME files and reports a clean secret scan over a fraction of the bundle. The two modules should not both exist in this shape: either `evaluateScannedFiles` delegates to `evaluateScannedFloor` with a bundle-file floor in `SCANNED_FLOORS`, or it keeps its own table and the shared helper grows the `REBUILD_HINT` variant it needs. Deciding which is a ten-minute call; leaving two near-identical premises is how one of them stops getting updated.

- **A floor measured once decays silently, and nothing says when it was last true** — `SCANNED_FLOORS` notes carry a date because the test demands one, but nothing compares that date, or the number beside it, against the tree it describes. `check-inline-hex` walks 212 files against a floor of 150; if the tree grows to 600 the floor is 25% of reality and stops catching the thing it exists for — a walk that lost two of three roots would pass. A second, LOOSE assertion in the other direction (fail when the actual count exceeds, say, 3× the floor, with the message "re-measure, this floor no longer describes the tree") turns quiet decay into a one-line chore. The registry test is the place; the number to compare against is already printed.

- **The floor lives beside the guard, not beside the walk, so a guard can still lie about what it counted** — `assertScannedFloor(CHECK_NAME, files.length)` trusts `files.length`, and every wrapper builds that array itself with a `catch { return }` swallowing unreadable directories per-directory. A walk that fails to read `app/` and succeeds on `lib/` reports the `lib/` count as if it were the whole scan; the floor catches the big version of that and not the version where one small root vanishes. Having `walkSources` return `{ files, unreadableDirs }` and failing on any unreadable directory is a stricter and simpler premise than a count — the count is a proxy for exactly this.

- **Nothing asserts the two wrappers' floors were measured from the SAME walk the wrapper performs** — the test reads both scripts as text and checks that `assertScannedFloor(CHECK_NAME, …)` appears; it cannot tell whether 150 was measured against `app+components+lib` or against something else entirely, because the measurement happened at a shell prompt and survives only as prose in a note. Running each guard once inside the registry test and asserting `scanned N` with `N >= minimum` would tie the number to a real execution — the same move the `repoWithBase` fixture made for the history guard, and the natural place is the third task of this section rather than a fourth.

- **`ScannedFloorError` is caught by an `instanceof` check in each wrapper, which breaks the moment tsx loads `lib/scanned-floor.ts` twice** — two module instances mean two distinct classes and an `instanceof` that answers false, at which point the wrapper rethrows and the guard fails with a stack trace instead of its one-line message. It has not happened (one tsx process, one resolution) but it is a fragile way to identify an error across a module boundary. A `code` string property on the error, checked instead of the class, is the version that cannot break, and it costs one line in each of the eleven wrappers this pattern is about to be copied into.

### Work-tree-premise follow-ups (2026-08-12)

- **The other eleven guards never ask what they are pointed at either** — `--is-inside-work-tree` fixed one script, and the premise it now states is not special to this one: `check-secrets.ts`, `check-migration-docs.ts` and `check-bundle-size.ts` all walk a tree from `path.join(__dirname, "..")` and would report a clean pass over an empty directory, because zero files with zero findings is what a pass looks like from inside. A shared `assertRealCheckout()` — the work-tree probe plus a floor on how many files the walk found — would make "I looked at nothing" a failure everywhere the way it now is here, and the twelve-guard registry is the natural place to hang it.

- **Nothing fails a guard that examined ZERO of the thing it guards** — `evaluatePrivacyBaselineProvenance` already refuses `checked === 0` ("a pass over zero baselines is not a pass"), which is exactly the right instinct and exists in exactly one of the twelve. The others count what they found and report it without ever comparing that count against a floor, so a glob that stops matching (a rename, a moved directory, a tightened `.gitignore`) reads as a clean run. One asserted minimum per guard, in the guard, is a smaller change than the report line each of them already prints.

- **The shallow-clone failure and the work-tree failure should be one probe with two answers** — both say "history is not available here", both are checked in different places by different means, and only one of them is reached on the path where `--base` resolved. A single `describeRepository()` returning `absent` / `shallow` / `full` up front, asserted once, would collapse two special cases into one premise and make the third state (`full`) the thing everything below is allowed to assume. It would also let the report say which of the three it saw on every run, which is the input the standing "nobody measures how often the drift half skips" suggestion needs.

- **`--is-inside-work-tree` answers `true` inside a `.git` directory's parent and also inside a submodule or a nested worktree** — the guard now knows it is in *a* work tree and not that it is in *this* repository, so a `PRIVACY_BASELINE_REPO_ROOT` pointing at any unrelated checkout still passes the probe and proceeds to the explicit-base requirement. `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` compared against the root the script was handed would close the gap between "a repository" and "the repository", and costs one more spawn on a path that already spawns six.

- **A `MANUAL-TASKS.md` entry for the two env vars** — `PRIVACY_BASELINE_BASE_REF` and `PRIVACY_BASELINE_REPO_ROOT` both change what this guard compares, both are documented only in a doc comment inside the script, and one of them can turn the drift half into a comparison against a stranger. The repo already keeps a file for "things a human must know before touching this", and the guard's failure messages are currently the only place either name appears outside the source.

### Scratch-repository harness follow-ups (2026-08-12)

- **The harness that makes one guard testable is worth exactly eleven more** — `repoWithBase` is thirty lines (mkdtemp, `git init`, two commits, return the base sha) and it is what turned two unreachable branches into assertions. Twelve entries sit in `LINT_GUARDS` and the other eleven are tested the way this one was: by reading their source with a regex and asserting the right strings appear in it. `lib/check-migration-docs.ts` and `check-supabase-migration-naming.ts` are the next best candidates — both are pure functions over a file tree, so a scratch directory (no git needed) would let their failure paths be run rather than pattern-matched. Lifting the helper into `__tests__/` as a shared fixture is the precondition.

- **Six seconds of the suite is now process startup** — the seven scratch-repository cases each pay a full `node --import tsx` boot (~430 ms) to assert a handful of strings, and every future guard given the same treatment adds its own. Running the script once per FIXTURE rather than once per assertion is already done; the next lever is a single long-lived tsx process driven over stdin, or an in-process entry point (`main(argv, env)` exported and called directly, with `spawnSync` reserved for the two cases that genuinely need a separate process — the `PATH=""` one and the exit-code ones).

- **The `PATH=""` case proves ENOENT and not the signal death beside it** — `git()` treats `run.error !== undefined` and `run.status === null` as the same hard failure, and only the first has a test. The second is what a SIGKILL from an OOM killer or a container CPU limit looks like, which is a far more likely production shape than a missing binary, and the message it produces (`killed by SIGKILL`) has never been rendered. A fixture `git` shim earlier on PATH that kills itself would cover it, and would also be the mechanism for testing a git that returns garbage on stdout.

- **Nothing asserts the guard is still wired into `lint:all`** — this run made the guard's own behaviour thoroughly covered while its reachability rests on one registry entry, and the parity test only checks that each `lint:*` script is registered OR exempt, so deleting the entry AND the script passes. The same hole the `unparseable` work closed one level down, and the standing suggestion below says so for all twelve; the new end-to-end harness makes the honest version cheap — run `lint:all` in a scratch checkout and assert the guard's name appears in its output.

### Baseline-revision follow-ups (2026-08-11)

- **The guard checks the table's provenance and not the guard's own presence** — `lint:baseline-provenance` is registered in `LINT_GUARDS`, and a commit that deletes the registry entry passes every check in the repo: the parity test only asserts that each `lint:*` script is registered OR exempt, and a removed script is neither. The same shape as the `unparseable` hole this run closed, one level up. Asserting the registry contains the entry (as `__tests__/privacy-baseline-provenance.test.ts` now does) covers the guard; nothing covers the other eleven.

- **`recordedOn` is compared as a string and never against reality** — `provenance_date_regressed` uses a lexicographic comparison, which is correct for `YYYY-MM-DD` and says nothing about whether the date is real: `2026-13-45` passes the format regex and orders fine. Parsing it (and rejecting a date in the future, which is how a copy-pasted placeholder shows up) would make the field a fact rather than a well-shaped string.

- **The note convention is enforced by the guard and documented nowhere a human reads first** — the failure message explains the `1171 → 980 (dropped the analytics section)` shape, which means the shape is learned by tripping over it. `MANUAL-TASKS.md` is where this repo puts "things a human must do"; a short entry on amending a policy file, naming the table and the convention, would move the discovery from a red build to the moment the policy is opened.

- **Nothing measures how often the drift half actually runs** — it now skips on a root commit, on a base predating the module, and (by design) never on a shallow clone, but the report prints those states and no one aggregates them. A one-line summary in the CI log is enough today; a guard whose skip rate nobody watches is the guard that has been skipping for a month.

### Baseline-provenance follow-ups (2026-08-11)

- **Nothing enforces the note convention on the entry that needs it least and the one that needs it most equally** — `note_omits_previous_words` requires the new note to contain the old count, which is the right forcing function for a SHRINK and pure ceremony for a growth of two words after a typo fix. The check has both numbers in hand and could scale its demand: a change inside the ±25% band the drift gate already tolerates is ordinary wording work, while a change that would have gone RED is the one whose note a reviewer actually reads. Requiring a longer note (or a structured `reason:` field) only past the band would put the friction where the risk is.

- **A `MANUAL-TASKS.md` entry would close the loop the guard opens** — the guard fails the build and tells the committer to write a note, but nothing tells the person amending a policy that a baseline exists until CI stops them. The repo already has a documented place for "things a human must do" and a lint guard (`lint:migration-docs`) that enforces one such convention by file; a short "amending a policy file" section, plus the same style of check over policy files, would move the discovery from a red build to the moment the file is opened.

- **The five translations still move independently, and the provenance now makes that legible** — a change to the shared Sentry disclosure ought to move all five translated baselines in one commit, and today each is checked only against its own previous value. With `recordedOn` recorded per entry, the cheap version is now available: assert the five non-English entries share a `recordedOn` whenever any of them changes, so a half-finished re-translation that updated `de` and left `es` at the old size is a failure rather than four files quietly disagreeing about which disclosure they translate.

- **The guard reads the working tree, so CI and a local run can disagree about what changed** — `changedFilesSince` diffs the base against the WORKING TREE, deliberately, so an uncommitted baseline edit is caught while the note is easiest to add. The cost is that a dirty tree makes the guard's answer depend on unstaged work: a developer who has a policy file open for unrelated reasons satisfies `policy_unchanged` without committing anything. Reporting whether the tree was dirty (one `git status --porcelain`) would make the difference visible in the log, and is the precondition for ever tightening the check to `<base>..HEAD` on CI.

### Size-baseline follow-ups (2026-08-11)

- **Character counts would make the six numbers comparable** — `de` renders the same disclosure in 169 words and `es` in 229, because German compounds what Spanish spells out, so one tolerance means six different amounts of real slack and the same 25% band is tighter on `de` than on any other file. Measuring characters (or calibrating a per-language multiplier off the current set) makes the band mean the same thing everywhere, and would let the tolerance be tightened without the shortest file setting the limit for all six.

- **Nothing checks the tolerance against the gap it has to fit into** — 25% was chosen against "no single section survives being dropped", which is a claim about the current documents that no test states. The English policy has a countable number of `<h2>` sections; asserting that the smallest of them is larger than 25% of the body would make the tolerance a measured fact the way the 0.9 similarity threshold is, instead of a number in a comment.

- **The five translations move together and the guard treats them as independent** — they are all the same Sentry disclosure, so a change to the disclosure ought to move all five baselines in one commit. One file drifting alone is a stronger signal than any of them drifting, and the per-file band cannot see it. Comparing each translation's ratio-to-its-baseline against the OTHERS' would catch a single half-finished re-translation that stayed inside its own band.

- **`missing_baseline` can never fire on a real build, which makes it a dead gate that reads as live** — `PRIVACY_PAGE_TARGETS` is derived from `PRIVACY_PAGE_LANGUAGES` and a test pins the baseline table's key set against that same list, so by the time a seventh language reaches `dist/` the suite has already gone red. That is the right outcome and it means the runtime code is unreachable by construction — worth either saying so in the comment (it is defence in depth against a caller passing its own target list) or moving the check to where a caller can actually trip it.

### Word-count-reporting follow-ups (2026-08-11)

- **Emit the counts as data, not only as prose** — `formatPrivacyPageWordCounts` renders `169-1171 words` for a human and `wordCounts` is dropped on the floor by the CLI. The `--json` suggestion below now has two things to carry (per-page word counts and, once the ratio work lands, per-page similarity), which is enough payload to make a machine-readable mode worth building rather than a nice idea.

- **The range hides the middle four pages** — min and max are two of six numbers, so `es` drifting from 229 to 175 moves nothing in the printed line as long as `de` stays at 169 and `en` at 1171. Printing all six (`en 1171, es 229, pl 188, be 185, ru 182, de 169`) is one more line in a log that already prints two, and it is the difference between "the extremes are unchanged" and "every page is where it was".

- **Count the ENGLISH page against its own history, separately from the translations** — the five translations are Sentry-disclosure subsets and the English file is the canonical full policy, so they are not members of one population: 1171 and 169 are both correct and a range spanning them is nearly uninformative — it is dominated by a gap that is *supposed* to be there, and the five translations it hides sit inside 169-229, a band 25× tighter. Splitting the report into `en 1171 words, translations 169-229` states the document relationship the whole check is built on and makes each half's drift legible on its own scale.

- **Give `evaluateBundleSmoke` the same treatment** — the privacy half now reports what it measured and the bundle half still prints `15 token(s) found across 2 chunk(s)`, which counts what it was *asked* about, not what it *found*. Chunk sizes are the number that would move on a dependency bloat or a Metro config change, they are already in hand (the script reads every chunk's text to search it), and the guard is the only place in the build that could notice a 280 kB chunk becoming 2 MB.

- **Give the canonical English policy a committed baseline size** — every content gate compares against `PRIVACY.md`, and the only thing under that file is the same 40-word floor as everything else. A bad merge that cut it from 1171 words to 200 passes every check, and then the ratio and the section comparisons all run against a document that lost most of itself — quietly, because the translations would still look different from it. A tracked expected word count, updated deliberately when the policy is amended, is the one guard the baseline file does not have.

- **Word counts are not comparable across the six languages** — the shipped set already shows it: `de` renders the same Sentry disclosure in 169 words and `es` in 229, because German compounds what Spanish spells out. One floor for all six therefore means six different amounts of slack, and any future per-language length check (the "much shorter than the English disclosure" suggestion below) inherits the same distortion. A character count, or a per-language multiplier calibrated on the current files, measures the thing both checks actually mean.

- **Assert each `PRIVACY.md.<code>` has exactly one `# ` heading** — `extractPrivacyPageBodyText` cuts at the FIRST `</h1>`, which is correct only while each source file has exactly one top-level heading. A second `# ` line folds that heading's text into the body, where it silently inflates the word count and joins the similarity comparison. Nothing states the premise and nothing checks it; one regex per file in the suite would keep the extractor's contract true rather than merely currently satisfied.

- **Have `build-spa-fallback.ts` refuse to WRITE a page that fails the content gates** — the gates live in a separate post-build guard, so a truncated or untranslated source file is rendered, written to `dist/`, and only then reported, three minutes and one script later. `lib/bundle-smoke.ts` is node-pure and already imported by the build's own module; calling `evaluatePrivacyPage` on each page before writing it would put the failure at the point of the mistake and keep a broken disclosure off disk entirely. The post-build guard stays either way — it is the only thing proving the file on disk is the file that was rendered.

### Near-copy threshold follow-ups (2026-08-11)

- **An all-pairs ratio needs a per-pair threshold, not the 0.9 constant** — the standing suggestion to compare translations against each OTHER (a `PRIVACY.md.be` copied from `PRIVACY.md.ru` passes today, since it differs from English) now has a measure to do it with, and reusing 0.9 unchanged would be wrong in both directions: `be` and `ru` share a large amount of vocabulary legitimately and already sit at 0.280 against each other — the highest pair in the set — while `de`/`es` sit near 0.2. A single constant either misses the copy it was written for or fails a real pair. A per-pair floor derived from the CURRENT measured matrix with slack (which is how 0.9 was chosen) is the same technique applied honestly.

- **Weight the ratio by rarity, so the words a policy cannot avoid stop counting** — the 0.157–0.280 that real translations score against English is almost entirely proper nouns, URLs, the effective date and product names: the tokens that survive translation by definition. Dropping words present in ALL six bodies before measuring would push real pairs toward 0 and leave copies at 1.0, widening a margin that is currently 0.28-to-0.9 and would become roughly 0.05-to-0.9. That matters most for the shortest translations, where a handful of shared proper nouns is a larger share of the body.

- **Carry the six measured ratios into the check's output** — the guard computes a number per page and prints a verdict, so nobody sees 0.28 drifting to 0.45 until the day it crosses 0.9 and the build goes red with no history to read. Pairs naturally with the standing `--json` mode suggestion for `check-bundle-smoke`: emitting the per-page ratio alongside the chunk count would let a future step diff them across runs, and would make the threshold's margin an observed fact on every build rather than a number measured once and written into a comment.

- **Move the prose gates off the build and into `npm test`** — `untranslated_heading`, `untranslated_body` and `near_english_body` all read rendered pages, but everything they need is a tracked `PRIVACY.md.<code>` and `renderPrivacyPage`, both of which the suite already imports and already runs over all six languages. Today the failure arrives from `lint:bundle-smoke` after a ~3-minute `expo export` in `verify`'s last leg; the same failure is available in the second leg in milliseconds. Keeping the dist-time copy is still right — it is the only thing proving the page that landed on disk is the page that was rendered — but the content questions do not have to wait for a build to be asked.

### Untranslated-body follow-ups (2026-08-11)

- **Assert each translation is a SUBSET of the English policy's section set, by count** — the five translated pages are Sentry-disclosure subsets of the canonical English document, and nothing states that relationship in code, so a translation with MORE `<h2>` sections than the English policy (a section invented in one language, or an English section pasted in twice) reads as fine. Counting rendered `<h2>`s per page and requiring the translations to sit at or below the English count is one number per page and encodes the document relationship the whole set is built on.

- **Reuse the body extractor to fail a page whose body is mostly the language picker** — `extractPrivacyPageBodyText` cuts at `</h1>`, which is correct for the current template and silently wrong if the picker is ever moved below the heading: the check would then compare six chrome-identical strings and pass everything. Asserting the extracted body does NOT contain every language label (the picker's fingerprint) would make that refactor fail loudly instead of hollowing the gate out.

- **Report all prose failures for a page, not the first one** — `evaluatePrivacyPages` deliberately stops at one failure per page so a wholly-English translation reports `untranslated_heading` rather than two rows saying the same thing. That is the right default and it hides a real distinction: with three or more comparisons (body similarity, section count, script range) the reader wants to know a page failed two of them, because one failing check is a mistake and three is a file that was never written. Collecting the codes and rendering `de: untranslated_heading, untranslated_body` on one line keeps the log short and stops discarding the signal.

- **Fail a translation whose rendered body is much SHORTER than the English disclosure section it mirrors** — every content check so far asks whether the text differs; none asks whether there is enough of it. A `PRIVACY.md.pl` truncated by a bad merge to its first paragraph differs from English, differs from the other translations, has a heading and a body, and passes everything. The five files are within a predictable band of each other today, so a floor derived from the shortest current translation (with slack) would catch the truncation class the whole guard still cannot see.

- **Compare each translation against the OTHER translations too, not only against English** — the baseline is the English page, so `PRIVACY.md.be` copied from `PRIVACY.md.ru` passes: it differs from English, which is all that is asked. Belarusian and Russian are the pair most likely to be copied and the pair a non-speaking reviewer is least likely to catch, so this is not a theoretical ordering of the language list. All-pairs over six headings is fifteen comparisons of strings already in memory.

- **Assert `<html lang>` matches the language the TEXT is in, using the script range** — `wrong_language` proves the attribute, `untranslated_heading` proves the text is not English, and neither proves the text is the language it claims. `PRIVACY.md.de` holding the Spanish policy passes both. A cheap script-range assertion (`ru`/`be` headings must contain Cyrillic; `de`/`es`/`pl`/`en` must not) is not language detection and does not pretend to be, but it separates the two alphabets the app ships and would have caught a be/ru swap.

- **Check the effective date line agrees across all six policy files** — every translation carries its own `_Effective date: …_` / `_Gültig ab: …_` line, currently 2026-07-04 in all six by hand. When the English policy is amended and the date bumped, five files keep the old one and the disclosure states a different effective date per language, which is the kind of inconsistency a regulator reads as two policies. The date is a single ISO string per file and grepping it is one regex.
